paras.en: Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.
paras.zh: 霍赫伯格：她能够考虑使用自己的手臂，用机械臂伸出来，拿起保温瓶，将其送到她的嘴边，然后将其朝她的嘴倾斜，然后将吸管放入她的嘴里，然后喝一口。虽然这不是近 15 年来她第一次喝东西，但这是她第一次真正能够完全按照自己的意愿喝东西。我记得她这样做时脸上的笑容。

paras.en: Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：几十年来，BrainGate 在很多方面取得了很多研究成功。但是说话呢？霍赫伯格说，在解码语音方面，这门科学还非常非常年轻。

paras.en: Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.
paras.zh: Hochberg：我们还处于早期阶段，需要非常明确。这是这个领域的开始。世界上只有极少数人拥有任何类型的可解码语音的植入式脑机接口。

paras.en: Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在解读谈话意图方面，科学处于什么位置？在过去的几集中，我们听到了失去说话能力的人的故事。其中之一就是凯西·哈雷尔（Casey Harrell），而凯西的大脑中也恰好植入了 BrainGate 设备。

paras.en: Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.
paras.zh: 凯西·哈雷尔：我叫凯西·哈雷尔，今年 47 岁。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西早上醒来，然后接通电源。

paras.en: Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.
paras.zh: Casey：可以这么说，我起床后通常要做的第一件事就是插入 Matrix。

paras.en: Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：他的意思是，将两根电线连接到从他头顶伸出的两个基座上。然后这两根黑线蜿蜒连接到附近的计算机。凯西大脑中的这些电极、来自他头部的电线和计算机统称为 BrainGate 2 神经接口系统。所以凯西把一切都点燃了，然后他就出发了。

paras.en: Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.
paras.zh: 凯西：除非我有医疗预约或需要离开家的事情，否则我会在一天的大部分时间里保持这个姿势，中间会有特别小的休息时间。

paras.en: Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西在思考说话时一直在产生大脑信号。这些是由凯西的神经元（特别是他的言语运动皮层中的细胞）发出的小而精确的电脉冲。还记得我们是如何了解到有超过 100 块肌肉参与言语的吗？这些是控制这些肌肉的大脑部分。

paras.en: Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.
paras.zh: 凯西：在过去的近两年里，我每周 7 天、每天使用解码器大约 10 到 14 个小时，这使我成为世界上人类已知的脑机接口的最大用户。

paras.en: Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has slowly taken away his ability to move and to talk.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：像朱尔斯一样，凯西也患有肌萎缩侧索硬化症。这种疾病慢慢地剥夺了他行动和说话的能力。

paras.en: Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. Then it became a slow motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me.
paras.zh: 凯西：2020年确诊后不久，我就开始失去说话的能力。然后，这变成了一场长达数年的慢动作车祸，直到几乎没有人能够理解我。

paras.en: By the time of my surgery, only my assistant and my wife, Levana, could really understand me fully. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.
paras.zh: 在我接受手术时，只有我的助手和我的妻子莱瓦娜（Levana）能够真正完全理解我。其他一些经常在附近的朋友应该能够理解我在说什么。我基本上依靠我的助手​​和我的妻子充当我向其他人提供翻译的工作。我没有去任何地方，甚至在没有他们的情况下进行视频通话，无论是其中一个还是两个。

paras.en: Sanders: In July of 2023, Casey volunteered for a clinical trial called BrainGate 2. A UC Davis neurosurgeon put four small electrical arrays onto the left side of Casey’s brain. I wanted to know more about how these arrays worked, so I talked to the neurosurgeon who put Casey’s devices into his brain.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：2023 年 7 月，凯西自愿参加了一项名为 BrainGate 2 的临床试验。加州大学戴维斯分校的神经外科医生在凯西的左侧大脑上放置了四个小型电子阵列。我想更多地了解这些阵列是如何工作的，所以我与将凯西的设备放入他大脑中的神经外科医生进行了交谈。

paras.en: David Brandman: My name is David Brandman, and I am the co-director of the UC Davis neuroprosthetics lab, developing next-generation neurotechnology to help people with paralysis. A brain-computer interface is a device that records brain signals from people that are paralyzed and then translates those brain signals to allow people to control objects in their environment using their minds.
paras.zh: 大卫·布兰德曼：我叫大卫·布兰德曼，是加州大学戴维斯分校神经修复实验室的联合主任，致力于开发下一代神经技术来帮助瘫痪患者。脑机接口是一种记录瘫痪者大脑信号的设备，然后翻译这些大脑信号，使人们能够用意念控制环境中的物体。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey’s implant is made of four arrays. Each of them are square and they’re about as wide as a peppercorn. Each array has a bunch of pointy ends that go down into his brain. They look a little like those metal cat brushes. Altogether, the four arrays contain 256 electrodes. These electrodes are all listening to Casey’s brain activity when he thinks about saying a word.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西的植入物由四个阵列组成。它们都是方形的，大约有花椒那么宽。每个阵列都有一堆尖头，深入他的大脑。它们看起来有点像那些金属猫刷。四个阵列总共包含 256 个电极。当凯西想要说一句话时，这些电极都会监听他的大脑活动。

paras.en: Brandman: The way this device works is by recording the electrical activity of the brain as he tries to speak.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：这个设备的工作原理是记录他试图说话时大脑的电活动。

paras.en: Sanders: The wires from Casey’s head carry those neural signals to nearby computers. That’s where machine learning algorithms attempt to do a very complex sort of matching. The algorithms match Casey’s brain activity patterns to the patterns that predictably occur with certain sounds called phonemes.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西头部的电线将这些神经信号传送到附近的计算机。这就是机器学习算法尝试进行非常复杂的匹配的地方。这些算法将凯西的大脑活动模式与某些称为音素的声音可预测出现的模式进行匹配。

paras.en: Brandman: We translate his brain signals into one of 39 different English phonemes. Now, a phoneme is a building block of language. So if I say the word hello, the word hello can be broken down into ha, uh, uhl, and oh. Hello.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：我们将他的大脑信号翻译成 39 种不同的英语音素之一。现在，音素是语言的组成部分。因此，如果我说“hello”这个词，那么“hello”这个词可以分解为“ha”、“uh”、“uhl”和“oh”。你好。

paras.en: Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：接下来，这些算法通过对凯西想说的话进行最佳猜测，将这些音素组装成单词。

paras.en: Brandman: So I translate this brain activity into a phoneme and then, using artificial intelligence, turn phonemes into words, words into sentences, and sentences into paragraphs.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：所以我将这种大脑活动转化为音素，然后使用人工智能将音素转化为单词，单词转化为句子，句子转化为段落。

paras.en: Sanders: So that’s the process, and it allows Casey to type messages on Slack, text his friends, and send emails. Sometimes in his emails to me, he includes a tagline at the bottom: “Sent from my brain,” with that cute little pink brain emoji. His setup also lets him convert these typed messages into spoken words. These words show up on a screen for him where Casey proofreads them. If everything looks good, Casey gives the go-ahead and the system speaks the words out loud. Brandman tells me that when Casey tries to speak naturally, he can say about six understandable words per minute. That’s pretty slow.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这就是这个过程，它允许凯西在 Slack 上输入消息、给他的朋友发短信以及发送电子邮件。有时，在他给我的电子邮件中，他会在底部添加一个标语：“从我的大脑发送”，并带有可爱的粉红色大脑表情符号。他的设置还可以让他将这些键入的消息转换为口头语言。这些文字出现在他的屏幕上，凯西对其进行校对。如果一切看起来都不错，凯西就会批准，系统就会大声说出这些话。布兰德曼告诉我，当凯西试图自然地说话时，他每分钟可以说大约六个可以理解的单词。那是相当慢的。

paras.en: Brandman: Using this prosthesis, he’s in the ballpark of 50 words per minute. Now, as I’m speaking to you right now, I’m speaking on the order of 120 to 150 words per minute, depending on how excited I am, right? So we’ve got him back to about a third of how quickly he spoke as an able-bodied person.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：使用这个假肢，他大约每分钟可以说 50 个单词。现在，正如我现在对你们讲话一样，我每分钟讲 120 到 150 个单词，具体取决于我的兴奋程度，对吗？因此，我们已经让他恢复了正常人说话速度的三分之一左右。

paras.en: Sanders: I had emailed Casey some questions a few days before our talk. But he didn’t answer them by email. He used his brain-computer interface to answer my questions in real time just by thinking about the words he wanted to say to me. As we introduced ourselves, I saw how the timescale had stretched.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在我们谈话前几天，我通过电子邮件向凯西发送了一些问题。但他没有通过电子邮件回复他们。他通过脑机接口实时回答我的问题，只需思考他想对我说的话。当我们自我介绍时，我发现时间已经被拉长了。

paras.en: Casey: It’s a challenge because we can have this conversation, but I am slower than the average Joe, even where we grew up.
paras.zh: 凯西：这是一个挑战，因为我们可以进行这样的对话，但我比普通人慢，即使在我们长大的地方也是如此。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey and I both grew up in the south, Casey in the Atlanta area and me in middle Tennessee. But he’s lived in the Bay Area for over 20 years now. And like me, his accent had faded.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西和我都在南部长大，凯西在亚特兰大地区，我在田纳西州中部长大。但他已经在湾区生活了 20 多年。和我一样，他的口音也消失了。

paras.en: Casey: And yes, I do not have much of a Southern accent anymore. But I love my roots, and I would love to show my daughter where and how I grew up. But it is exceedingly difficult to travel when you cannot move.
paras.zh: 凯西：是的，我不再有太多南方口音了。但我爱我的根，我很乐意向我的女儿展示我在哪里以及如何长大。但当你无法移动时，旅行就变得非常困难。

paras.en: Sanders: Before his mobility was limited, Casey did a lot of cool things.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在行动受限之前，凯西做了很多很酷的事情。

paras.en: Casey: I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the Earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it. I am very fortunate because I have been able to do something that I love and also develop some deep friendships and relations with other phenomenal people.
paras.zh: 凯西：我职业生涯的大部分时间都是作为气候活动家，并走遍了全球，与破坏地球的公司作斗争，并试图为我们的星球和居住在地球上的人们伸张正义。我很幸运，因为我能够做我喜欢的事情，并与其他杰出的人建立了深厚的友谊和关系。

paras.en: Sanders: My interview with Casey was unlike any I’ve ever had. I’m used to being flexible for interviews. There’s time zone problems, language barriers, mathematicians who sometimes answer my questions in symbols and formulas. But when I logged on to Zoom to talk with Casey, I quickly realized this conversation would be different. I was self-conscious at the beginning of our talk. I fumbled around too much. I’d ask Casey a question and then another one before he had a chance to answer. I accidentally interrupted him a few times. Sometimes I wasn’t sure if he was composing an answer or just waiting for me to say something else. This poor performance on my part wasn’t unusual for Casey at all.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：我对凯西的采访与我以往接受过的采访都不一样。 I’m used to being flexible for interviews.有时区问题、语言障碍、数学家有时用符号和公式回答我的问题。但当我登录 Zoom 与凯西交谈时，我很快意识到这次谈话会有所不同。在我们谈话开始时我很不自在。 I fumbled around too much.在凯西有机会回答之前，我会问他一个问题，然后再问另一个问题。 I accidentally interrupted him a few times.有时我不确定他是在写答案还是只是在等我说别的话。我的糟糕表现对凯西来说并不罕见。

paras.en: Casey: It is hard for people in your position to stay focused because you were not used to the cadence of a conversation this slowly.
paras.zh: 凯西：对于你这个职位的人来说，很难保持专注，因为你不习惯如此缓慢的谈话节奏。

paras.en: Sanders: He’s right. I was not used to it. And timing, in conversations and in life, is everything. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：他是对的。我不习惯。在谈话和生活中，时机就是一切。这是加州大学洛杉矶分校的格雷格·布莱恩特的报道。

paras.en: Bryant: Turns, conversational turns, happen at the level of hundreds of milliseconds at the longest. Two hundred milliseconds is a long turn. That’s a fifth of a second. I mean, that’s really fast. So if you are slow at all, it’s noticeable. We have to coordinate our talk so our terms make sense. I can’t take too long or be too quick to respond to your questions. I have to know when to stop and start. We get into this flow, kind of a dynamic, and that is hugely consequential for how we feel about the conversation, the other person, ourselves. You know, it’s all timing.
paras.zh: 布莱恩特：对话，对话的轮转，最长发生在数百毫秒的水平。两百毫秒是一个漫长的转弯。那是五分之一秒。我的意思是，这真的很快。因此，如果你的速度很慢，就会很明显。我们必须协调我们的谈话，以便我们的条款有意义。我不能花太长时间或太快来回答你的问题。我必须知道何时停止和开始。我们进入这种流动状态，一种动态，这对于我们对谈话、对方和我们自己的感受非常重要。你知道，这一切都是时机。

paras.en: Sanders: Let’s turn to Jules. His words start in his brain too, but then they take a different route. He types them by looking at letters on a screen, then his voice clone says them. It’s also a slow process and one that takes a lot of mental power, too. At one point in our conversation, MA describes the effort this requires of Jules.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：我们来谈谈朱尔斯。他的话语也从他的大脑中开始，但随后却走了不同的路线。他通过查看屏幕上的字母来输入它们，然后他的声音克隆说出它们。这也是一个缓慢的过程，也需要大量的精神力量。在我们的谈话中，MA 描述了 Jules 需要付出的努力。

paras.en: MA: And in his brain, you know, you can imagine he’s doing all these mental gymnastics, to, right now, he’s listening to us. He’s writing something with his eyes, like letter by letter to contribute to the conversation. Plus, he has the answers that he pre-wrote, of the questions that you asked. So it really is like, there’s a whole lot happening behind the scenes that of course anybody who doesn’t have to think about their voice takes for granted. So I’ll pause to let him complete what he’s saying.
paras.zh: MA：在他的大脑中，你知道，你可以想象他正在做所有这些心理体操，现在他正在听我们说话。他正在用眼睛写一些东西，比如一个字母一个字母地写，以促进对话。另外，他还预先写好了您提出的问题的答案。所以，实际上，幕后发生了很多事情，当然，任何不需要考虑自己声音的人都会认为这是理所当然的。所以我会停下来让他完成他所说的。

paras.en: Sanders: MA and I wait here for Jules to weigh in. So far you’ve heard ten seconds of the pause. The full length of the pause was a minute and 18 seconds.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：妈妈和我在这里等朱尔斯发表意见。到目前为止，你已经听到了十秒钟的停顿。整个暂停时间为一分十八秒。

paras.en: Jules: It is a challenge to communicate with people who don’t interact with me on a daily basis. I have a major bottleneck from my thoughts to actually speaking.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：与那些不每天与我互动的人沟通是一个挑战。从我的想法到实际说话，我遇到了一个很大的瓶颈。

paras.en: Sandes: And as with Casey, these pauses can introduce difficulties. Here’s speech pathologist Jessica Pietrowski with more on that.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：和凯西一样，这些停顿可能会带来困难。言语病理学家杰西卡·皮特罗斯基 (Jessica Pietrowski) 对此有更多了解。

paras.en: Pietrowski: Humans are not very comfortable with silence, especially communication. And when we’re talking to one another, we fill in the silences, it’s less awkward. And so, someone who’s communicating with a device is probably very used to those latency periods and some more silence and they’re comfortable with it. Whereas the person they’re communicating with is like, let’s keep it going, like this is, I want to help, I want to fill in the blanks, I don’t want this to feel awkward, but in turn, might make it a little more awkward than they think.
paras.zh: Pietrowski：人类不太适应沉默，尤其是交流。当我们互相交谈时，我们会填补沉默，这样就不那么尴尬了。因此，与设备通信的人可能非常习惯这些等待时间和更多的沉默，他们对此感到很舒服。而与他们交流的人却说，让我们继续下去，就像这样，我想提供帮助，我想填补空白，我不想让这感觉尴尬，但反过来，可能会让事情比他们想象的更尴尬。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules hates when people read his screen before he’s ready to say what he wants. This particular hate inspired a joke in his stand-up routine.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯讨厌人们在他准备好说出他想说的话之前阅读他的屏幕。这种特殊的仇恨在他的脱口秀节目中引发了一个笑话。

paras.en: [Jules audio]: People read off my screen while I’m typing and try to finish what I am saying. It’s like having to constantly deal with an over-competitive charades partner.
paras.zh: [Jules 音频]：当我打字时，人们会从我的屏幕上读出内容，并尝试完成我所说的内容。这就像必须不断地与竞争过度的猜字游戏伙伴打交道。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules and Casey encounter other people’s impatience constantly. Not that it isn’t well-intentioned but still, it does not help. Even worse, they face other people’s misconceptions about what they’re capable of. Casey is an interesting, funny and compelling conversationalist. That might not be apparent to everyone who doesn’t slow down to hear him. And that’s an assumption that really bothers him.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯和凯西经常遇到其他人的不耐烦。并不是说它不是出于好意，但它仍然没有帮助。更糟糕的是，他们面临着其他人对他们能力的误解。凯西是一位有趣、风趣且引人注目的健谈者。对于那些不放慢速度听他讲话的人来说，这一点可能并不明显。这个假设确实让他困扰。

paras.en: Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.
paras.zh: 凯西：医疗保健系统如此迅速地对待我，这是非常不尊严的，也是一个可怕的后果。

paras.en: Sanders: Brandman has seen this dismissal, this mistreatment too. It happens with some of the volunteers he works with on the BrainGate 2 project I mentioned earlier. That’s the same trial Casey’s in.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：布兰德曼也看到过这种解雇和虐待。我之前提到的与他一起参与 BrainGate 2 项目的一些志愿者身上就发生过这种情况。这与凯西所参加的审判相同。

paras.en: Brandman: I think as healthcare professionals, we conflate the inability to communicate with the lack of understanding. And I’ve witnessed this firsthand as I’ve watched doctors and nurses interact with my BrainGate participants and then treat them as if they are invalid. Or they’re not there because they’re unable to express themselves. And in fact, I go out of my way in the intensive care unit on the wards and dealing with anyone who’s dealing with my participants to say, look, you know, they’re inside. They’re there. They can understand everything that’s happening. They just happen to not be able to speak. And so please treat them with the respect and dignity that they deserve. And it’s a constant challenge for the participants that I work with. And it’s the reality of which we face and it’s the bias that we have against people that can’t speak for themselves.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：我认为作为医疗保健专业人员，我们将无法沟通与缺乏理解混为一谈。我亲眼目睹了这一点，因为我看到医生和护士与我的 BrainGate 参与者互动，然后像对待病人一样对待他们。或者他们不在那里是因为他们无法表达自己。事实上，我在病房的重症监护室里不遗余力地对待任何与我的参与者打交道的人，说，看，你知道，他们在里面。他们就在那里。他们可以理解正在发生的一切。他们只是碰巧无法说话。因此，请给予他们应有的尊重和尊严。对于与我一起工作的参与者来说，这是一个持续的挑战。这就是我们面临的现实，这就是我们对那些不能为自己说话的人的偏见。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey and the other people with ALS are not alone. Many people who have trouble talking or who just need more time can be judged this way. Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西和其他患有 ALS 的人并不孤单。许多说话有困难或者只是需要更多时间的人都可以这样判断。这是来自 Bridging Voice 的卡琳娜·纳金 (Karina Nagin) 的报道。

paras.en: Nagin: It’s how people see you. And so when you have ALS and you cannot move and you don’t even have facial expressions and you’re hooked up to machines, people assume you’re not there. And we see this every day where people either don’t talk to the person with ALS, assuming that they can’t respond. They speak really loudly and slow. Their mind is completely working.
paras.zh: 纳金：这就是人们如何看待你。因此，当你患有肌萎缩侧索硬化症（ALS）时，你无法移动，甚至没有面部表情，而且你还连接着机器，人们会认为你不在那里。我们每天都会看到这样的情况：人们要么不与 ALS 患者交谈，认为他们无法做出回应。他们说话声音很大而且很慢。他们的头脑完全运转。

paras.en: Sanders: For now, Casey’s words may be slow. But despite all the drawbacks, they are still an absolute marvel. Remember Hochberg from the start of this episode? He’s one of the neuroscientists who works with Casey, and he told me a story from the first few days of testing after Casey’s BCI was implanted.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：目前来看，凯西的话可能会很慢。但尽管有这些缺点，它们仍然是一个绝对的奇迹。还记得本集一开始的霍赫伯格吗？他是与凯西一起工作的神经科学家之一，他给我讲了凯西脑机接口植入后最初几天测试的故事。

paras.en: Hochberg: We gave him a 50-word vocabulary on day one. And even on day one, he was able to say some key sentences from those 50 high-value words.
paras.zh: Hochberg：第一天我们就给了他 50 个单词的词汇。即使在第一天，他就能说出这 50 个高价值单词中的一些关键句子。

paras.en: Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在测试的这个阶段，凯西被要求说出一些预先指定的句子，以便研究人员可以测试他们的系统。

paras.en: Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.
paras.zh: 凯西：大多数句子都是我们所说的闭环。

paras.en: Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这意味着研究人员已经知道什么大脑活动模式应该与凯西想要说的话相匹配。这是一个测试，看看系统是否正常工作。

paras.en: Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”
paras.zh: 凯西：解码器将能够验证我是对还是错，给我预先加载的简短句子。我被要求说：“那有什么好处？”

paras.en: Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：“那有什么好处？”这并不是有史以来最令人心酸的一句话，但它在房间里和通过视频远程加入的研究人员中产生了很大的影响。

paras.en: Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.
paras.zh: 凯西：“那有什么好处？”当我成功后，每个人都在哭泣。

paras.en: Sanders: Later on, there was time for Casey to actually express himself.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：后来凯西有时间真正表达自己的想法。

paras.en: Casey: It was only after the first few sessions that I had any real time to say what I wanted for a good amount of time in relative privacy. That said, it was pure joy, even though I wasn’t getting to say what I wanted to say in that moment. It was a profound moment for me. The possibilities for the near future, for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.
paras.zh: 凯西：只有在最初的几次会议之后，我才有时间在相对私密的情况下在相当长的时间内说出我想要的内容。也就是说，这是纯粹的快乐，尽管我当时没能说出我想说的话。这对我来说是一个意义深远的时刻。对于我和其他人来说，不久的将来的可能性是难以想象的。

paras.en: Sanders: Things only got better from there. To set the scene here, during this session, Hochberg was in his office and Casey was at his home, sitting in his living room. Hochberg was watching Casey on a screen.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：从那时起事情只会变得更好。为了设置这里的场景，在这次会议期间，霍赫伯格在他的办公室里，凯西在他的家里，坐在他的客厅里。霍赫伯格正在屏幕上看着凯西。

paras.en: Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. That is, the decoders and the AI and the machine learning language models would be able to select from basically a full dictionary. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.
paras.zh: Hochberg：在第二次会议上，回来后给了他完整的 125,000 多个单词的英语词典供他选择。也就是说，解码器、人工智能和机器学习语言模型将能够从基本上完整的字典中进行选择。他说的第一句话是这样的：“这个东西开着吗？”有点有趣的说法。

paras.en: The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.
paras.zh: 使用脑机接口的第二天，他说的下一句话，或者说我们解码的第二件事是，“我在寻找猎豹。”而且已经是第二天了。我们知道存在各种解码错误的机会。当我看到这一点时，我说，你知道，使用植入脑机接口的第二天的第二句话不可能说任何关于猎豹的事情。你知道，这显然是一个解码错误，但没关系。

paras.en: Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：霍赫伯格可以在屏幕上看到凯西，但他看不到房间里刚刚发生的真正重要的事情。

paras.en: Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.
paras.zh: 霍赫伯格：他四岁的女儿刚刚打扮成猎豹走进房间。

paras.en: Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这是凯西回忆起的同一时刻。

paras.en: Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Everyone was thinking that it must have been a mistake that I could not use this language. It was so random. This was only from the people like Leigh who were not in the room with us. The researchers who were there could validate that, yes, I said this. I meant it because of the unique context.
paras.zh: 凯西：是的，这一次我记得很清楚。这是我在 2024 年 8 月上旬经历的第二次谈话。我女儿穿着猎豹装，非常可爱。这是她最喜欢的动物之一。他们正在经历一个阶段，他们所做的一切都非常快，从一件事跑到另一件事。每个人都认为我不会使用这种语言一定是一个错误。真是太随意了。这只是来自像 Leigh 这样的人，他们没有和我们一起在房间里。那里的研究人员可以证实，是的，我说过这一点。我这么说是因为独特的背景。

paras.en: Sanders: It’s one of those moments that many parents have. A kid does something cute, a parent plays along. But in this moment for Casey and his child, it was anything but ordinary.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这是许多父母都会经历的时刻之一。孩子做一些可爱的事情，父母也跟着一起玩。但此刻对于凯西和他的孩子来说，这绝非平常。

paras.en: Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.
paras.zh: 霍赫伯格：她是在他被诊断出患有肌萎缩侧索硬化症的时候出生的。人们可以想象，因为从电脑中传出的声音是他自己声音的一个版本，然后剩下的互动就发生在爸爸和女儿之间。而且是父母和孩子之间的事。

paras.en: Sanders: The BCI had given Casey something priceless, a minute to play with his sweet little cheetah.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：BCI 给了凯西一些无价的东西，那就是和他可爱的小猎豹玩耍的一分钟。

paras.en: Casey: I was quietly confident that it would work the way it ended up working for me. I had done a lot of research and the thing was that the technology was on the cusp of a breakthrough. And why not me? I asked myself.
paras.zh: 凯西：我暗自相信它会以最终为我工作的方式发挥作用。我做了很多研究，事实是这项技术正处于突破的边缘。为什么不是我呢？我问自己。

paras.en: Sanders: Early on in the research project, Casey and his wife had been told not to expect it to work. This was an experiment and the outcome was far from certain. Casey, however, was optimistic.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在研究项目的早期，凯西和他的妻子被告知不要指望它会起作用。这是一个实验，结果还远未确定。然而，凯西却很乐观。

paras.en: Hochberg: So to me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living, not only key kind of instrumental activities of daily living, but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child. They’re going to restore communication between friends and family and care partners and health care providers.
paras.zh: 霍赫伯格：所以对我来说，看到它如此迅速和强大地发挥作用，确实强调了这些技术不仅能够恢复日常生活活动，不仅能够恢复日常生活的关键工具性活动，而且它们还将恢复父母和孩子之间的沟通。他们将恢复朋友、家人、护理伙伴和医疗保健提供者之间的沟通。

paras.en: Sanders: Because this is a podcast about the human voice, I’ve been asking people I interview what their voice means to them. Here’s Casey’s answer.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：因为这是一个关于人类声音的播客，所以我一直在问我采访的人他们的声音对他们意味着什么。这是凯西的回答。

paras.en: Casey: It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.
paras.zh: 凯西：这意义重大。我认为这是我在整个疾病中失去的最重要的东西。

paras.en: Sanders: Getting it back, even in a limited form, is everything.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：收回它，即使是以有限的形式，也是一切。

paras.en: Casey: It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond, respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life up to that point.
paras.zh: 凯西：能够从一开始就被理解，能够与我的女儿交谈和回应，回应我的女儿，这真是太神奇了，特别是因为在那之前我的生活完全缺乏这一点。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey’s restored voice changed his life.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西恢复的声音改变了他的生活。

paras.en: Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary. And to look back on my previous answer, it is something that really can still improve.
paras.zh: 凯西：这是养育女儿的能力。这是与我妻子联系的能力。这是与朋友开玩笑的能力。时机就是一切，这就是为什么什么都没有，这是完全革命性的。回顾一下我之前的回答，确实还有待改进。

paras.en: Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Those hours felt like a huge gift at the time, considering that they hadn’t been able to talk meaningfully for a long time. Here’s Brandman.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在实验开始时，研究团队告诉凯西和他的妻子，他们可以尝试使用脑机接口进行每周几个小时的休闲聊天。考虑到他们已经很长时间无法进行有意义的交谈，这些时间在当时感觉就像是一份巨大的礼物。这是布兰德曼。

paras.en: Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. And it got to a point where Casey wanted to use the system to say all the things that he wanted to say.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：随着我们每周去他家两三次，事情变得越来越好。凯西想用这个系统说出他想说的所有事情。

paras.en: Sanders: Early on, only the researchers could set Casey up with the system, plugging him into the Matrix, as he puts it.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：早期，只有研究人员可以设置凯西的系统，将他插入矩阵，正如他所说。

paras.en: Brandman: And so our research technologist would start coming to his house three, four, five times a week to don and doff the system to enable him to communicate so that he could go about his day. And so at a certain point, we saw, well, he really wants to use the system. Can we streamline this for him? And so we petitioned the FDA to actually allow us to change the clinical trial protocol slightly so that we could train his care partners to don and doff the system without us being there. And so since then, he’s been a near daily user of the system.
paras.zh: 布兰德曼：因此，我们的研究技术专家会开始每周去他家三、四、五次，穿上和脱下系统，使他能够进行交流，以便他可以度过自己的一天。所以在某个时候，我们看到，他真的很想使用这个系统。我们可以为他简化这个过程吗？因此，我们请求 FDA 实际上允许我们稍微改变临床试验方案，以便我们可以训练他的护理伙伴在我们不在场的情况下穿脱系统。从那时起，他几乎每天都使用该系统。

paras.en: Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. I’m going to read you some numbers from a research paper Brandman and his colleagues published about Casey’s BCI in Nature Neuroscience in June of 2026.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这与每周工作几个小时相差甚远。我将向您朗读布兰德曼和他的同事于 2026 年 6 月在《自然神经科学》杂志上发表的关于凯西脑机接口的研究论文中的一些数据。

paras.en: “Over nearly two years, the participant, that’s Casey, used the BCI for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present to maintain rich, interpersonal communication with his family and friends, independently control his personal computer, and sustain full-time employment, despite being paralyzed. He communicated 183,060 sentences, totaling 1,960,163 words, at an average rate of 56 words per minute. He labeled 92 percent of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.”
paras.zh: “近两年来，参与者凯西在没有研究人员在场的情况下在家中使用脑机接口超过 3,800 个小时，尽管瘫痪了，但仍然与家人和朋友保持丰富的人际沟通，独立控制自己的个人电脑，并维持全职工作。他传达了 183,060 个句子，总计 1,960,163 个单词，平均速度为每分钟 56 个单词。他将 92% 的句子标记为至少大部分被正确解码。”

paras.en: Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. They’re messages to his daughter, jokes with his partner, texts to his friends. They’re games of Wordle with his wife and kid. Here’s Casey and his family in a video shot by UC Davis Health.
paras.zh: 老实说，这些数字以这种非常简单的科学方式来说是枯燥的。但当你停下来思考时，你就会发现，这近两百万个单词中的每一句话，每一个字，都是连接凯西和他生活的一根绳索。它们是给他女儿的信息、与他的伴侣的笑话、给他的朋友的短信。他们是和他的妻子和孩子玩Wordle 游戏。这是加州大学戴维斯分校健康中心拍摄的视频中的凯西和他的家人。

paras.en: Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.
paras.zh: 好吧，所以没有 A，但我们得到了 E.M-I。 O.M-I。干得好，团队。我们快到了。

paras.en: Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. He’s got some bells and whistles up his sleeve.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：我们在这里讨论了很多关于言语的问题，以及凯西的 BCI 恢复他说话能力的基本方法。但凯西的脑机接口比这更进一步。这让他有能力添加一些额外的东西。他有一些花里胡哨的东西。

paras.en: Casey: It is really a communication device, first and foremost, and less of a tool that I use to make funny remarks. But I do have that as well in my repertoire. For example, I have the ability to add sound effects to what I am saying.
paras.zh: 凯西：首先，它实际上是一种通信设备，而不是我用来发表有趣言论的工具。但我的保留曲目中也确实有这个。例如，我有能力为我所说的话添加声音效果。

paras.en: Sanders: For instance, Casey has a sad trombone sound.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：例如，凯西有悲伤的长号声音。

paras.en: Casey: So if I find something funny and want to say, LOL, the theme from the TV show, Seinfeld, will play.
paras.zh: 凯西：所以如果我发现一些有趣的事情并且想说，哈哈，电视节目《宋飞正传》的主题就会播放。

paras.en: Sanders: This is what he means. These jokes make me think of Jules, which made me wonder if Casey, like Jules, could also swear with his system.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这就是他的意思。这些笑话让我想起了朱尔斯，这让我想知道凯西是否也可以像朱尔斯一样用他的系统发誓。

paras.en: Casey: To answer your question of whether I can curse with this device, I most certainly [beep] can.
paras.zh: 凯西：回答你的问题，我是否可以用这个设备咒骂，我肯定可以[嘟嘟]可以。

paras.en: Sanders: So for all your inquiring minds, there you have it. Looking ahead a bit, there’s a lot happening on the horizon. The science here is moving fast and many companies are working on similar systems. We’re going to cover that in a few episodes. But for now, Casey is alone. He is an N of 1, as the scientists say – the only person using a brain-computer interface for communication this heavily.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：对于所有好奇的人来说，这就是你想要的。展望未来，将会发生很多事情。这里的科学发展很快，许多公司正在开发类似的系统。我们将在几集中介绍这一点。但现在，凯西孤身一人。正如科学家所说，他是 N of 1——唯一一个如此频繁地使用脑机接口进行交流的人。

paras.en: Casey: I hope to have this changed very soon because I feel like everyone who wants this should have the opportunity to have it, especially those who are with my disease.
paras.zh: 凯西：我希望这种情况很快就能改变，因为我觉得每个想要这个的人都应该有机会拥有它，特别是那些患有我的疾病的人。

paras.en: Sanders: Hochberg tells me that this drive to help others is common among people who volunteer for these sorts of clinical trials.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：霍赫伯格告诉我，这种帮助他人的动力在自愿参加此类临床试验的人中很常见。

paras.en: Hochberg: Each participant in the trial has been just so generous and so clear that they recognize that it’s early days in the research, but they’ve told us that they want to help other people with paralysis. They want to be able to allow people with brainstem stroke or cervical spinal cord injury or ALS or other paralyzing illnesses or injuries to have improved function, to be able to regain control over that computer or regain the fluent speech and communication that they had previously. So it’s that generosity of spirit that has really defined the participants in our BrainGate studies.
paras.zh: 霍赫伯格：试验中的每个参与者都非常慷慨和明确，他们认识到研究还处于早期阶段，但他们告诉我们他们想帮助其他瘫痪患者。他们希望能够让患有脑干中风、颈脊髓损伤、肌萎缩侧索硬化症或其他瘫痪疾病或损伤的人改善功能，能够重新控制计算机或恢复以前流畅的言语和交流。因此，正是这种慷慨的精神真正定义了我们 BrainGate 研究的参与者。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey’s generosity, his drive to help other people, really shines through as we talk. But I want to get back to him. I ask Casey what it’s been like to have this technology in his home, in his brain. He tells me how precious our voices are, and how easy it is for many of us to forget that.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在我们谈话的过程中，凯西的慷慨和帮助他人的动力真正体现出来。但我想回到他身边。我问凯西，在他的家里、他的大脑中拥有这项技术感觉如何。他告诉我，我们的声音是多么宝贵，而我们很多人却很容易忘记这一点。

paras.en: Casey: We take them for granted. The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now, and we should have accelerated approval for devices like this.
paras.zh: 凯西：我们认为它们是理所当然的。当您跑步并想要释放压力时能够尖叫。在伴侣耳边说甜言蜜语的能力。这些就是生活的全部内容。当你的那些时光被剥夺时，你会不惜一切代价想要把它们夺回来。这就是为什么现在这已经足够好了，我们应该加速批准这样的设备。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey’s BCI is slow compared to the pace of a normal conversation. And it gets things wrong occasionally.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西的脑机接口比正常对话的速度慢。而且偶尔也会出错。

paras.en: Casey: Sorry, I am trying to answer you. And it is changing what I want to say. And I am being stubborn instead of trying to say it another way, which I will do now.
paras.zh: 凯西：抱歉，我正在尝试回答你。它正在改变我想说的内容。我很固执，而不是试图用另一种方式表达，我现在就会这么做。

paras.en: [Sanders audio] I’m not in any rush. You take as much stubborn time as you want.
paras.zh: [桑德斯音频]我并不着急。你想花多少顽固的时间就花多少时间。

paras.en: Sanders: And it needs an internet connection and power. And let’s not forget that Casey has an adapter coming out of the top of his head. But these are solvable problems, one that scientists are actively working on. So not perfect, but as Casey puts it, good enough for now.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：它需要互联网连接和电源。我们不要忘记凯西的头顶上有一个适配器。但这些都是可以解决的问题，科学家们正在积极研究这一问题。所以并不完美，但正如凯西所说，目前已经足够好了。

paras.en: Scientific efforts to restore voices have been transformative for Jules, Casey, and others. But the ability to separate a voice from a body also raises new possibilities for our societies and for our lives.
paras.zh: 恢复声音的科学努力对朱尔斯、凯西和其他人来说是变革性的。但将声音与身体分离的能力也为我们的社会和我们的生活带来了新的可能性。

paras.en: MA: His voice will live on in whatever videos or things we’ve captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally, and that’s as far as that goes.
paras.zh: MA：他的声音将永远存在于我们捕捉到的任何视频或事物中，无论他故意留给我们什么，仅此而已。

paras.en: Sanders: On the next episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into a strange new digital world where voices might not be what they seem.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在下一集中，我们将走出实验室，进入一个奇怪的新数字世界，那里的声音可能并不像看上去的那样。

paras.en: Hany Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time. And somehow those are coexisting.
paras.zh: 哈尼·法里德：我认为，我们生活在一个激动人心的时代和一个可怕的时代。不知何故，这些是共存的。

paras.en: Sanders: What changes are coming in a world where voices can be so easily cloned?
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在一个声音可以轻易克隆的世界里，将会发生什么变化？

paras.en: Farid: Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.
paras.zh: Farid：如今，只需键盘和互联网连接，您就可以打字，并且可以获得任何内容的图像、声音、视频，任何人都在做或说任何事情。

paras.en: Sanders: The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Shute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund with support from PRX.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：深渊是《科学新闻》的制作。它基于我劳拉·桑德斯的原创报道。本集由 Ella Rowen 制作和混音。我们的项目经理是阿什利·耶格尔。南希·舒特是我们的主编。我们的音乐是由 Blue Dot Sessions 制作的。该播客的部分制作是由 Burroughs Wellcome 基金在 PRX 的支持下完成的。

paras.en: This podcast was produced with support from the Burroughs Wellcome Fund and in partnership with PRX. The podcast logo was created by Neil Webb.
paras.zh: 该播客是在 Burroughs Wellcome 基金的支持下并与 PRX 合作制作的。播客徽标由尼尔·韦伯创建。

articles.title: Mice With Parkinson's-Like Brain Changes Unexpectedly Recovered a Year Later
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: Three weeks of exposure to a pesticide left laboratory mice moving slowly and struggling to balance.
paras.zh: 接触杀虫剂三周后，实验小鼠行动缓慢，难以保持平衡。

paras.en: Scientists were using the chemical to study some of the movement problems seen in Parkinson's disease. But as they continued watching the animals after exposure ended, those problems began to ease.
paras.zh: 科学家们正在使用这种化学物质来研究帕金森病中出现的一些运动问题。但当他们在暴露结束后继续观察这些动物时，这些问题开始缓解。

paras.en: Without receiving a treatment to reverse their symptoms, the mice gradually improved. By the end of a year, they performed movement tests as well as controls of the same age.
paras.zh: 在没有接受治疗来扭转症状的情况下，小鼠的症状逐渐好转。到一年年底，他们进行了运动测试以及同龄对照。

paras.en: Neuroscientist Xuelin Lou of the Medical College of Wisconsin told ScienceAlert that the resolution of these Parkinson's-like deficits was "totally unexpected."
paras.zh: 威斯康星州医学院的神经科学家薛林楼告诉 ScienceAlert，这些帕金森氏症样缺陷的解决“完全出乎意料”。

paras.en: In a study published in iScience, Lou and colleagues, cell biologist Prince Joshi and physiologist Fan Fan, investigated what happened long after exposure to the pesticide rotenone ended.
paras.zh: 在《iScience》杂志上发表的一项研究中，Lou 及其同事、细胞生物学家 Prince Joshi 和生理学家 Fan Fan 研究了在接触杀虫剂鱼藤酮后很久之后发生的情况。

paras.en: Parkinson's damages cells that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement. Rotenone reproduces some features of the disease in animals by interfering with the tiny energy-producing structures inside cells, called mitochondria.
paras.zh: 帕金森氏症会损害产生多巴胺的细胞，多巴胺是一种有助于控制运动的化学物质。鱼藤酮通过干扰细胞内微小的能量产生结构（称为线粒体），在动物身上重现该疾病的一些特征。

paras.en: Exposure to rotenone and certain other pesticides has also been associated with a higher risk of Parkinson's in people. However, these associations alone don't establish causation.
paras.zh: 接触鱼藤酮和某些其他杀虫剂也与人们患帕金森病的风险较高有关。然而，这些关联本身并不能确定因果关系。

paras.en: Most experiments using rotenone models focus on the early effects.
paras.zh: 大多数使用鱼藤酮模型的实验都关注早期效应。

paras.en: The researchers gave young adult male mice daily rotenone injections for 21 days. Control mice received the same injection mixture without the toxin.
paras.zh: 研究人员连续 21 天每天给年轻成年雄性小鼠注射鱼藤酮。对照小鼠接受相同的不含毒素的注射混合物。

paras.en: Within four weeks of the experiment's start, exposed mice traveled shorter distances, moved more slowly, and struggled to stay on a rotating rod used to assess balance and coordination. They also spent less time exploring the open, unwalled arms of an elevated maze, a measure of anxiety-like behavior.
paras.zh: 在实验开始后的四个星期内，暴露的小鼠移动的距离更短，移动速度更慢，并且难以留在用于评估平衡和协调性的旋转杆上。他们还花更少的时间探索高架迷宫的开放、无围墙的手臂，这是一种类似焦虑行为的衡量标准。

paras.en: The longer follow-up revealed a gradual change.
paras.zh: 较长的随访显示出逐渐的变化。

paras.en: In the open-field movement test, exposed mice reached control-group levels within about four months. By seven months, their rotating-rod performance was no longer significantly different from that of controls. At 12 months, the groups also performed similarly in anxiety-related tests.
paras.zh: 在旷场运动测试中，暴露的小鼠在大约四个月内达到了对照组的水平。七个月后，他们的旋转杆性能与对照组不再有显着差异。 12 个月时，各组在焦虑相关测试中也表现相似。

paras.en: Brain tissue offered a possible clue. The researchers examined a movement-related midbrain region called the substantia nigra pars compacta.
paras.zh: 脑组织提供了可能的线索。研究人员检查了一个与运动相关的中脑区域，称为黑质致密部。

paras.en: They identified dopamine-producing cells using an enzyme needed to make dopamine, called tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). Early after exposure, the number and density of cells detectable with this marker were about 40 percent lower in exposed mice.
paras.zh: 他们使用一种产生多巴胺所需的酶（称为酪氨酸羟化酶（TH））来鉴定产生多巴胺的细胞。暴露后不久，暴露小鼠中用该标记物可检测到的细胞数量和密度降低了约 40%。

paras.en: However, a second marker that labels neurons more broadly showed that total neuronal density was preserved.
paras.zh: 然而，更广泛地标记神经元的第二个标记表明总神经元密度得以保留。

paras.en: "Our findings suggest that they just lose their identity," Lou said.
paras.zh: “我们的研究结果表明，他们只是失去了自己的身份，”卢说。

paras.en: Some surviving cells may have produced too little TH to be identified as dopamine-producing neurons. Their disappearance from the TH-positive count didn't establish that they had died.
paras.zh: 一些幸存的细胞可能产生的 TH 太少，无法被识别为产生多巴胺的神经元。他们从 TH 阳性计数中消失并不能证明他们已经死亡。

paras.en: At 12 months, TH-positive cell counts and density were comparable between groups, although the enzyme signal remained weaker in exposed mice.
paras.zh: 12 个月时，尽管暴露小鼠的酶信号仍然较弱，但各组之间的 TH 阳性细胞计数和密度相当。

paras.en: Aging complicated that comparison. Control mice examined at 12 months had about 45 percent lower TH-positive cell density than controls examined early on. In exposed mice, that density changed little between the two measurements. Lou said the reason for this difference wasn't known.
paras.zh: 老龄化使这种比较变得复杂。 12 个月大时检查的对照小鼠的 TH 阳性细胞密度比早期检查的对照小鼠低约 45%。在暴露的小鼠中，两次测量之间的密度变化很小。卢表示，造成这种差异的原因尚不清楚。

paras.en: These tissue measurements came from different animals at each time point. Both groups also declined in rotating-rod performance as they aged, so matching older controls did not mean returning to their younger condition.
paras.zh: 这些组织测量结果来自每个时间点的不同动物。随着年龄的增长，两组人的旋转杆表现也会下降，因此与年长的对照组相匹配并不意味着恢复到年轻时的状态。

paras.en: Lou explained that the recovery likely reflects both better function in the remaining dopamine-producing neurons and their resistance to age-related loss. Separating those contributions is difficult because the methods could not track individual neurons over time.
paras.zh: 楼解释说，这种恢复可能反映了剩余的产生多巴胺的神经元的更好的功能以及它们对与年龄相关的损失的抵抗力。分离这些贡献是很困难的，因为这些方法无法随着时间的推移跟踪单个神经元。

paras.en: The recovery mechanism isn't clear. Lou said possibilities worth exploring include surviving neurons growing new branches, adjustments in their connections, and changes linking cellular metabolism to gene activity. The team is now studying what drives this resilience.
paras.zh: 恢复机制尚不清楚。卢说，值得探索的可能性包括幸存的神经元长出新的分支、调整它们的连接，以及将细胞代谢与基因活动联系起来的变化。该团队目前正在研究是什么推动了这种弹性。

paras.en: Other scientists have tested an experimental drug combination for Parkinson's-like symptoms in mice. Here, the behavioral differences resolved without such an intervention.
paras.zh: 其他科学家已经在小鼠身上测试了一种实验性药物组合，用于治疗帕金森氏症样症状。在这里，行为差异在没有这种干预的情况下得到了解决。

paras.en: Only male mice were studied, with three to eight animals per group in the 12-month analyses, depending on the measurement.
paras.zh: 仅对雄性小鼠进行了研究，根据测量结果，在 12 个月的分析中每组有 3 到 8 只动物。

paras.en: The mouse models lacked several features of human Parkinson's, including significant accumulation of an abnormally modified form of the protein alpha-synuclein. Rotenone can also cause muscle weakness and general illness that influence movement tests.
paras.zh: 小鼠模型缺乏人类帕金森氏症的几个特征，包括α-突触核蛋白异常修饰形式的显着积累。鱼藤酮还会导致肌肉无力和影响运动测试的一般疾病。

paras.en: Lou cautioned that "the findings do not mean that pesticide exposure is harmless or disprove the association between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's disease risk."
paras.zh: 楼警告说，“研究结果并不意味着接触农药是无害的，也不意味着接触农药与帕金森病风险之间存在关联。”

paras.en: "The conclusion from this work should not be directly extrapolated to patients or workers under risk," Lou said.
paras.zh: “这项工作的结论不应直接推断到处于危险中的患者或工人，”楼说。

paras.en: Establishing the findings' relevance to humans will require evidence from people or studies of human dopamine-producing cells and tissues.
paras.zh: 确定这些发现与人类的相关性需要来自人类的证据或对人类产生多巴胺的细胞和组织的研究。

paras.en: The research has been published in iScience.
paras.zh: 该研究已发表在 iScience 上。

articles.title: 2.8 Million Eels Have Gathered Around a Single Deep-Sea Mountain Off The Coast of Australia
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: Every year, hundreds of meters below the waves in the cold, dark waters off southeast Australia, a wondrous gathering takes place.
paras.zh: 每年，在澳大利亚东南部寒冷、黑暗的海水中，海浪以下数百米处，都会发生一次奇妙的聚会。

paras.en: Around a lonely mountain south of Tasmania called Patience Seamount, millions of eels converge, transforming a normally quiet patch of the deep sea into a seething morass of writhing, sinuous bodies.
paras.zh: 塔斯马尼亚南部一座名为“耐心海山”的孤山周围，数以百万计的鳗鱼聚集在一起，将原本平静的深海变成一片沸腾的沼泽，里面布满了蜿蜒的身体。

paras.en: These deep-sea creatures are basketwork eels (Diastobranchus capensis), and scientists believe they're gathering for one of the most important events of their lives – reproduction.
paras.zh: 这些深海生物是篮鳗（Diastobranchus capensis），科学家相信它们聚集在一起是为了生命中最重要的事件之一——繁殖。

paras.en: Now, a study led by marine scientist Ben Scoulding of Australia's CSIRO has quantified the astonishing scale of this mysterious congregation for the first time.
paras.zh: 现在，由澳大利亚联邦科学与工业研究组织（CSIRO）的海洋科学家本·斯库丁（Ben Scoulding）领导的一项研究首次量化了这个神秘群体的惊人规模。

paras.en: At its peak, Scoulding and his colleagues have determined, the gathering could contain as many as 2.8 million eels, collectively weighing more than 3,500 metric tons (3,860 US tons).
paras.zh: 斯考丁和他的同事们确定，在高峰期，鳗鱼群中可能含有多达 280 万条鳗鱼，总重量超过 3,500 公吨（3,860 美吨）。

paras.en: Yet one enormous question lingers: Why, of all the relatively similar nearby mountains under the ocean, do the eels choose this one?
paras.zh: 然而，有一个巨大的问题仍然存在：为什么在海底附近所有相对相似的山脉中，鳗鱼选择了这座？

paras.en: "That's one of the biggest unanswered questions," Scoulding told ScienceAlert.
paras.zh: “这是最大的悬而未决的问题之一，”斯考丁告诉 ScienceAlert。

paras.en: "Patience is one of around 120 seamounts in the Huon and Tasman Fracture marine parks south of Tasmania, and although nearby seamounts have similar depths and broad environmental characteristics, they don't support the same aggregation of eels.
paras.zh: “耐心是塔斯马尼亚南部休恩和塔斯曼断裂海洋公园中约 120 个海山之一，尽管附近的海山具有相似的深度和广泛的环境特征，但它们并不支持同样的鳗鱼聚集。

paras.en: "At this stage, we have some good hypotheses, but we don't yet have a definitive answer."
paras.zh: “现阶段，我们有一些很好的假设，但我们还没有明确的答案。”

paras.en: Teasing apart the true scale of the annual basketwork eel aggregation at Patience Seamount is the work of decades.
paras.zh: 厘清耐心海山一年一度的编织鳗鱼聚集的真实规模是几十年的工作。

paras.en: Unusual numbers of the eels in the area had been reported by commercial fisheries since at least the 1980s and 1990s, but it wasn't until 2007 that a deep-sea camera survey finally captured the extraordinary gathering on film.
paras.zh: 至少从 20 世纪 80 年代和 1990 年代起，商业渔业就报告称该地区鳗鱼的数量异常多，但直到 2007 年，深海摄像机调查才最终在电影中捕捉到了这一非凡的聚集现象。

paras.en: The seamount lies within the Huon Marine Park, established in 2007 as an expansion of an earlier marine reserve created in 1999 to protect the region's fragile deep-sea ecosystems.
paras.zh: 这座海山位于休恩海洋公园内，该公园成立于 2007 年，是 1999 年创建的早期海洋保护区的扩展，旨在保护该地区脆弱的深海生态系统。

paras.en: As part of a 2007 expedition to survey the seabed and marine life in and around the marine park, CSIRO scientists towed a camera behind a research vessel – like the bear going over the mountain – to see what they could see.
paras.zh: 作为 2007 年调查海洋公园及其周围海底和海洋生物的探险活动的一部分，CSIRO 的科学家在一艘研究船后面拖曳了一台相机（就像熊越过山一样），看看他们能看到什么。

paras.en: In contrast to the bear, however, they saw much more than the other side of the mountain.
paras.zh: 然而，与熊相比，他们看到的远不止山的另一边。

paras.en: In the permanent darkness deep beneath the waves, the water column roiled with eels.
paras.zh: 在海浪深处永久的黑暗中，鳗鱼在水柱中翻腾。

paras.en: Subsequent surveys shed further light. The eels inhabit the seamount year-round, but their numbers peak in the southern autumn months, from March to May. Eels caught during this peak have been found in advanced spawning condition – both male and female – strongly indicating a reproductive reason for the eel jamboree.
paras.zh: 随后的调查进一步揭示了这一点。鳗鱼全年栖息在海山上，但其数量在南部秋季的三月至五月达到高峰。在此高峰期间捕获的鳗鱼被发现处于提前产卵状态（无论是雄性还是雌性），强烈表明鳗鱼盛会的繁殖原因。

paras.en: "Although seamounts are well known as hotspots where fish can aggregate, it's unusual to find millions of fish concentrated around a single feature. Patience Seamount itself is relatively small, covering only about 2 square kilometers [0.8 square miles], yet it consistently supports an enormous seasonal aggregation over many months," Scoulding said.
paras.zh: “虽然海山是众所周知的鱼类聚集热点，但数以百万计的鱼类集中在一个地物周围的情况并不常见。耐心海山本身相对较小，仅覆盖约 2 平方公里（0.8 平方英里），但它始终支持数月内巨大的季节性聚集，”斯考丁说。

paras.en: "Seeing so much biomass concentrated on such a small deep-sea feature is rare, and the scale, persistence, and likely reproductive nature of the aggregation make it one of the most remarkable fish aggregations documented in the deep ocean."
paras.zh: “看到如此多的生物量集中在如此小的深海特征上是罕见的，这种聚集的规模、持久性和可能的​​繁殖性质使其成为深海中记录的最显着的鱼类聚集之一。”

paras.en: But observing an extraordinary eel swarm is one thing. Working out just how many are there is not as simple.
paras.zh: 但观察到非凡的鳗鱼群是一回事。计算出有多少人并不那么简单。

paras.en: A 2021 paper on the aggregation used hydroacoustic measurements and on-camera eel counts to estimate that tens of thousands of eels may have been present during an April 2015 aggregation.
paras.zh: 2021 年一篇关于聚集的论文使用水声测量和摄像机上的鳗鱼计数来估计，在 2015 年 4 月的一次聚集期间可能存在数万条鳗鱼。

paras.en: Scoulding and his colleagues wanted to address the question with intent and precision.
paras.zh: 斯考丁和他的同事希望有针对性地、精确地解决这个问题。

paras.en: "What nobody knew was how large the aggregation was, how long it persisted, or how many eels were actually involved," he said. "One of the main aims of our study was to answer those questions."
paras.zh: “没有人知道聚集的规模有多大，持续了多长时间，或者实际上涉及了多少条鳗鱼，”他说。 “我们研究的主要目的之一就是回答这些问题。”

paras.en: Between 2023 and 2025, the researchers conducted a series of surveys around Patience Seamount, using sonar to map the enormous concentrations of fish in the water.
paras.zh: 2023 年至 2025 年间，研究人员在耐心海山周围进行了一系列调查，利用声纳绘制了水中鱼类的大量分布图。

paras.en: But there was a complication. Basketwork eels aren't the only fish that gather around Patience Seamount. Orange roughy (Hoplostethus atlanticus) also congregate there, and sonar alone can't distinguish between the two.
paras.zh: 但有一个复杂的情况。篮鳗并不是唯一聚集在耐心海山周围的鱼类。橙色粗糙鱼（Hoplostethus atlanticus）也聚集在那里，仅靠声纳无法区分两者。

paras.en: So the team combined their acoustic measurements with underwater camera footage, which allowed them to work out how much each species was contributing to the sonar signal.
paras.zh: 因此，该团队将声学测量与水下摄像机镜头结合起来，这使他们能够计算出每个物种对声纳信号的贡献程度。

paras.en: Their findings revealed an aggregation of jaw-dropping proportions. At its largest, the swarm extended roughly 3 kilometers long, 2 kilometers wide, and 150 meters above the seafloor (1.9 miles long by 1.2 miles wide, and 492 feet high).
paras.zh: 他们的发现揭示了令人瞠目结舌的比例的集合。最大时，虫群大约长 3 公里，宽 2 公里，距海底 150 米（长 1.9 英里，宽 1.2 英里，高 492 英尺）。

paras.en: The researchers estimated that the biomass of basketwork eels increased from around 750 metric tons in March to more than 3,500 metric tons in May.
paras.zh: 研究人员估计，篮鳗的生物量从 3 月份的约 750 吨增加到 5 月份的 3,500 多吨。

paras.en: "The sheer size of it was remarkable. Estimating that there could be up to 2.8 million eels and more than 3,500 tons of biomass concentrated around a single seamount really highlights just how extraordinary Patience Seamount is," Scoulding said.
paras.zh: “它的规模之大令人惊叹。据估计，一座海山周围可能集中有多达 280 万条鳗鱼和超过 3,500 吨生物量，这确实凸显了耐心海山的非凡之处，”斯库丁说。

paras.en: And, he noted, by combining their new data with previous surveys, the researchers were able to document the aggregation's presence from December to August.
paras.zh: 他指出，通过将新数据与之前的调查相结合，研究人员能够记录从 12 月到 8 月期间聚集的情况。

paras.en: "The thing that surprised me most was the persistence of the aggregation. We knew it existed, but we didn't expect it to be present for so much of the year."
paras.zh: “最让我惊讶的是这种聚集的持续性。我们知道它的存在，但我们没想到它会在一年中的大部分时间里出现。”

paras.en: The composition of the gathering also changes throughout the year. At some times, orange roughy make up a substantial proportion of the fish; at others, basketwork eels overwhelmingly dominate.
paras.zh: 聚会的组成也在一年中发生变化。有时，橙色粗糙鱼占鱼类的相当大比例；在其他地方，编篮鳗鱼占据压倒性优势。

paras.en: The two species even seem to prefer different parts of the mountain. Orange roughy tend to gather around the steeper upper slopes, while basketwork eels prefer the deeper, flatter terrain around its base.
paras.zh: 这两个物种甚至似乎更喜欢山上的不同部分。橙色粗糙鱼倾向于聚集在较陡的上坡周围，而编织鳗鱼则喜欢在其底部周围更深、更平坦的地形。

paras.en: What makes Patience Seamount so attractive to the eels, however, remains unclear. One possibility, the researchers noted, is its proximity to the continental shelf, which may influence fish movement or the currents flowing around the mountain.
paras.zh: 然而，是什么让耐心海山对鳗鱼如此有吸引力，目前尚不清楚。研究人员指出，一种可能性是它靠近大陆架，这可能会影响鱼类的活动或山周围的水流。

paras.en: Whatever the reason, the gathering underscores the importance of protecting these remote deep-sea habitats.
paras.zh: 无论出于何种原因，这次聚会强调了保护这些偏远深海栖息地的重要性。

paras.en: Patience Seamount was once subjected to bottom trawling, but scientists are now seeing encouraging signs of recovery, including rebuilding orange roughy populations and the return of living corals to previously trawled areas.
paras.zh: 耐心海山曾经遭受过海底拖网捕捞，但科学家们现在看到了令人鼓舞的复苏迹象，包括重建橙色粗糙鱼种群以及活珊瑚返回到以前拖网捕捞的地区。

paras.en: And there is still much to learn about the eels themselves. Scoulding and his team found further evidence that they're gathering to reproduce, including females carrying advanced eggs and sporting empty bellies.
paras.zh: 关于鳗鱼本身，还有很多东西需要了解。斯考丁和他的团队发现了更多证据表明它们正在聚集繁殖，包括雌性携带先进的卵并空腹。

paras.en: This introduced an unexpected wrinkle to the research. The eels may stop feeding as they prepare to spawn – and an eel that isn't hungry is unlikely to take the bait. From among the writhing mass of eels deep below their boat, the researchers only managed to catch seven.
paras.zh: 这给研究带来了意想不到的困难。鳗鱼在准备产卵时可能会停止进食，而不饥饿的鳗鱼不太可能上钩。在船下深处扭动的鳗鱼群中，研究人员只捕获了七条。

paras.en: And they have yet to establish exactly when and where spawning takes place.
paras.zh: 他们还没有确定产卵的确切时间和地点。

paras.en: Understanding that process – and how the aggregation changes from year to year – could help scientists determine what these fascinating animals need to thrive.
paras.zh: 了解这个过程——以及每年的聚合如何变化——可以帮助科学家确定这些迷人的动物需要什么才能茁壮成长。

paras.en: "Because the aggregation occurs within a protected marine park, it provides a rare opportunity to revisit the site every few years and see how the population changes through time," Scoulding said.
paras.zh: 斯考丁说：“由于这种聚集发生在受保护的海洋公园内，因此提供了一个难得的机会，可以每隔几年重新访问该地点，看看种群数量随时间的变化。”

paras.en: "If the ecosystem continues to recover from historical fishing impacts, we may see further increases in the size of the aggregation."
paras.zh: “如果生态系统继续从历史捕鱼影响中恢复，我们可能会看到聚集规模进一步扩大。”

paras.en: The research has been published in Royal Society Open Science.
paras.zh: 该研究已发表在《皇家学会开放科学》杂志上。

articles.title: "Record High": 146 Experts Call to Declare Climate Change a Global Health Emergency
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: As record heat interrupts work, overloads hospitals, and claims thousands of lives around the world, international experts are calling for climate change to be officially recognized as a global health emergency, in The Lancet's 2026 Countdown on Health and Climate Change.
paras.zh: 由于创纪录的高温导致世界各地的工作中断、医院超负荷运转并夺去了数千人的生命，国际专家在《柳叶刀》的 2026 年健康与气候变化倒计时中呼吁将气候变化正式视为全球卫生紧急事件。

paras.en: The report shows risks and harms associated with extreme heat and droughts continue to rise faster than climate action, despite growing investment in the transition away from fossil fuels across the past decade.
paras.zh: 报告显示，尽管在过去十年中对化石燃料转型的投资不断增加，但与极端高温和干旱相关的风险和危害的上升速度继续快于气候行动。

paras.en: "The rate of increase in many climate-related health threats is accelerating, while heat deaths linked to climate change have reached a record-high, and the economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," says climate health researcher Marina Romanello, executive director of The Lancet Countdown.
paras.zh: 《柳叶刀倒计时》执行主任、气候健康研究员玛丽娜·罗曼内洛表示：“许多与气候相关的健康威胁正在加速增长，而与气候变化相关的高温死亡人数已创历史新高，经济损失对脆弱部门和社区的打击最为严重。”

paras.en: It's been 10 years since the first Countdown report was published, bringing together experts in public health, climate, energy, data, economics, and more, to track the impacts of climate change on 54 different health indicators.
paras.zh: 自第一份倒计时报告发布以来已有 10 年了，该报告汇集了公共卫生、气候、能源、数据、经济学等领域的专家，追踪气候变化对 54 项不同健康指标的影响。

paras.en: The authors of the latest report are seriously concerned about how slow the international community has been to make the changes necessary to protect human health.
paras.zh: 最新报告的作者对国际社会在为保护人类健康做出必要改变方面进展缓慢感到严重关切。

paras.en: "A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world's response to them, and in many cases even accelerating," Romanello says.
paras.zh: 罗曼内洛说：“《巴黎协定》签署十年后，我们的研究结果十分明确：气候变化对健康的危害增长速度超过了世界应对气候变化的速度，在许多情况下甚至还在加速。”

paras.en: "Real progress has been made in clean energy, health system readiness, and health-protective regulation, all of which are already delivering health benefits to local communities.
paras.zh: “在清洁能源、卫生系统准备和健康保护监管方面已经取得了真正的进展，所有这些都已经为当地社区带来了健康益处。

paras.en: "However, progress has been too slow, too small, and isn't reaching those who need it most. That is why we are calling for climate change to be formally recognized as a global health emergency, with health placed at the center of every climate decision."
paras.zh: “然而，进展太慢、太小，而且没有惠及最需要的人。这就是为什么我们呼吁将气候变化正式视为全球卫生紧急情况，并将健康置于每项气候决策的中心。”

paras.en: In 2023, 71.5 percent of heat-related deaths worldwide can be attributed to climate change. The total was 710,000; if it weren't for climate change, that number would be around 200,000, according to estimates.
paras.zh: 到 2023 年，全球 71.5% 的高温相关死亡可归因于气候变化。总数为71万；据估计，如果不是气候变化，这一数字将达到 20 万左右。

paras.en: Between 2016 and 2023, an estimated 540,800 deaths each year were linked to heat. Climate change was responsible for 68 percent of them (369,900), which is a big jump from 55 percent of heat-linked deaths per year in the previous decade, 2006-2015.
paras.zh: 2016 年至 2023 年间，估计每年有 540,800 人死于高温。其中 68%（369,900 人）是由气候变化造成的，这比过去 2006 年至 2015 年的十年中每年因高温导致的死亡人数 55% 大幅上升。

paras.en: In 2025, heat cost global economic productivity around US$1.07 trillion just by interrupting people's ability to work, with the greatest losses seen in the GDP of countries in Southeast Asia and Africa.
paras.zh: 2025年，仅仅因为高温影响了人们的工作能力，全球经济生产力就损失了约1.07万亿美元，其中东南亚和非洲国家的GDP损失最大。

paras.en: Globally, agriculture and construction industries were particularly hard-hit by heat-related losses, because they depend on people doing physically demanding work outdoors.
paras.zh: 在全球范围内，农业和建筑业受到与高温相关损失的打击尤其严重，因为它们依赖于人们在户外进行体力劳动。

paras.en: The human body has its limits, and increasingly, the conditions outdoors are becoming unbearable, if not lethal.
paras.zh: 人体有其局限性，户外条件即使不是致命的，也越来越难以忍受。

paras.en: "These numbers point to a clear emergency," says Romanello.
paras.zh: “这些数字表明存在明显的紧急情况，”罗曼内洛说。

paras.en: "The risks become even more profound when you consider how different hazards interact and compound. At the same time, drought is spreading, and the world is swinging to water extremes, some drying out, while others are flooding."
paras.zh: “当你考虑到不同的危害如何相互作用和复合时，风险就会变得更加严重。与此同时，干旱正在蔓延，世界正在走向极端缺水，一些地区干旱，另一些地区则发生洪水。”

paras.en: Drought can quickly lead to food shortages and malnutrition, poor water and air quality, and mental health issues, while floods put people at greater risk of infectious, respiratory, and digestive diseases. Both of these extremes put already-stretched health systems under strain.
paras.zh: 干旱会迅速导致粮食短缺和营养不良、水和空气质量差以及心理健康问题，而洪水则使人们面临更大的传染病、呼吸道和消化系统疾病的风险。这两种极端情况都使本已捉襟见肘的卫生系统面临压力。

paras.en: Meanwhile, by 2040 the world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are planning to exceed fossil fuel production by 150 percent of what would be needed to keep global warming below 1.5°C.
paras.zh: 与此同时，到 2040 年，全球 100 家最大的石油和天然气公司计划将化石燃料产量提高 150%，以将全球变暖幅度控制在 1.5°C 以下。

paras.en: The researchers lay out a plan to address the crisis.
paras.zh: 研究人员制定了解决危机的计划。

paras.en: They say the World Health Organization and United Nations must declare climate change a global health emergency, coordinate governments to put human health at the center of climate decisions, and increase grant-based funding to finance climate and health initiatives.
paras.zh: 他们表示，世界卫生组织和联合国必须宣布气候变化为全球卫生紧急事件，协调各国政府将人类健康置于气候决策的中心，并增加基于赠款的资金，为气候和健康举措提供资金。

paras.en: They also say global governments must "prioritize and promote the urgent,
paras.zh: 他们还表示，全球政府必须“优先考虑并促进紧迫的、

paras.en: just, and equitable reduction of greenhouse gas emissions as a global health imperative".
paras.zh: 公正、公平地减少温室气体排放是全球健康的当务之急"。

paras.en: "Ten years ago, we proposed that responding to climate change could offer the greatest health opportunity of the 21st century through adaptation efforts and rapid progress in phasing down fossil fuels and other emission sources", says global health expert and The Lancet Countdown co-chair Anthony Costello.
paras.zh: 全球卫生专家、《柳叶刀倒计时》联合主席安东尼·科斯特洛表示：“十年前，我们提出，通过适应努力以及逐步减少化石燃料和其他排放源方面的快速进展，应对气候变化可以提供 21 世纪最大的健康机会。”

paras.en: "A decade on, we have proof that health-centered climate action works: cleaner air, more resilient healthcare and warning systems are protecting health and saving lives globally. But the pace and scale of emissions reduction remains entirely out of step with the pace and scale of the harm."
paras.zh: “十年过去了，我们有证据表明，以健康为中心的气候行动是有效的：更清洁的空气、更有弹性的医疗保健和预警系统正在保护全球健康并拯救生命。但减排的速度和规模仍然与危害的速度和规模完全不同步。”

articles.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world

paras.en: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
paras.zh: 杀死恐龙的小行星可能帮助蚂蚁征服了世界

paras.en: Scientists discover that mysterious âjumping genesâ may have helped ants take over the world after the dinosaurs disappeared.
paras.zh: 科学家发现，神秘的“跳跃基因”可能帮助蚂蚁在恐龙消失后占领了世界。

paras.en: - The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from âjumping genesâ hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.
paras.zh: - 杀死恐龙的小行星可能为蚂蚁征服地球奠定了基础，隐藏在蚂蚁 DNA 中的“跳跃基因”带来了令人惊讶的推动力。科学家发现，这些移动遗传元素的爆发性活动与主要蚂蚁群体的崛起同时发生，可能有助于增强它们通过气味进行交流的非凡能力。

paras.en: Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck Earth and brought the age of the dinosaurs to an end. The mass extinction that followed created opportunities for countless other animals to evolve and spread. Ants were among the groups that eventually became remarkably successful, and scientists have now identified a surprising genetic factor that may have helped fuel their rise.
paras.zh: 大约 6600 万年前，一颗小行星撞击地球，结束了恐龙时代。随后的大规模灭绝为无数其他动物的进化和传播创造了机会。蚂蚁是最终取得巨大成功的群体之一，科学家现在发现了一个令人惊讶的遗传因素，可能有助于推动它们的崛起。

paras.en: Today, ants are the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found around the world. New research published in Science Advances suggests that their extraordinary evolutionary success was partly driven by mobile segments of DNA known as transposable elements, or "jumping genes."
paras.zh: 如今，蚂蚁是最大的社会性昆虫家族，在世界各地发现了超过 15,000 种蚂蚁。发表在《科学进展》上的新研究表明，它们非凡的进化成功部分是由被称为转座元件或“跳跃基因”的 DNA 移动片段驱动的。

paras.en: The international study was led by Dr. Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity (IEB) at the University of Münster (Germany).
paras.zh: 这项国际研究由德国明斯特大学进化与生物多样性研究所 (IEB) 的 Lukas Schrader 博士领导。

paras.en: Jumping genes are pieces of DNA that can move to different locations within a genome and produce additional copies of themselves. Scientists once viewed them primarily as "genomic parasites" because, much like viruses, they can multiply without providing any clear benefit to their host. In some cases, their activity can even contribute to disease.
paras.zh: 跳跃基因是 DNA 片段，可以移动到基因组中的不同位置并产生自身的额外副本。科学家们曾经将它们主要视为“基因组寄生虫”，因为它们就像病毒一样，可以在不给宿主带来任何明显好处的情况下繁殖。在某些情况下，它们的活动甚至会导致疾病。

paras.en: More recently, however, researchers have begun recognizing that these mobile genetic elements can also create opportunities for evolutionary change. The new findings suggest they played an important role in the remarkable diversification of ants.
paras.zh: 然而，最近，研究人员开始认识到这些可移动的遗传元件也可以为进化变化创造机会。新发现表明它们在蚂蚁的显着多样化中发挥了重要作用。

paras.en: When the scientists compared different groups of ants, they discovered that lineages containing the greatest numbers of jumping genes also tended to have the most species today.
paras.zh: 当科学家比较不同的蚂蚁群体时，他们发现含有最多数量跳跃基因的谱系往往也拥有最多的物种。

paras.en: Even more revealing was the timing of these genetic changes. The researchers found that several major ant lineages experienced separate surges in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene (about 66 million years ago). These bursts occurred shortly before the groups began expanding into the thousands of species that exist today.
paras.zh: 更能说明问题的是这些基因变化的时间。研究人员发现，几个主要的蚂蚁谱系在古近纪早期（约 6600 万年前）经历了跳跃基因活性的单独激增。这些爆发发生在这些群体开始扩展到当今存在的数千种物种之前不久。

paras.en: "The asteroid impact had dramatic consequences for the environment. We have now found the genomic mechanism that connects these ecological upheavals to the subsequent rapid diversification of the ants: transposable elements," explains Lukas Schrader.
paras.zh: “小行星撞击对环境产生了巨大的影响。我们现在发现了将这些生态剧变与蚂蚁随后的快速多样化联系起来的基因组机制：转座因子，”卢卡斯·施拉德解释道。

paras.en: Ants are not the only animals showing this evolutionary pattern. Previous studies have also identified periods of increased jumping gene activity associated with the emergence of new species in other groups, including primates and bats.
paras.zh: 蚂蚁并不是唯一表现出这种进化模式的动物。先前的研究还发现，跳跃基因活性增加的时期与其他群体（包括灵长类动物和蝙蝠）中新物种的出现有关。

paras.en: The researchers also discovered a connection between jumping genes and the expansion of gene families that allow ants to communicate through chemical signals.
paras.zh: 研究人员还发现跳跃基因与基因家族的扩展之间存在联系，这些基因家族使蚂蚁能够通过化学信号进行交流。

paras.en: Of particular importance were genes responsible for odorant receptors, which enable ants to detect and respond to smells. These receptors are essential to nearly every aspect of ant social behavior. Ants depend heavily on chemical cues to find their way through the environment, identify members of their own colonies, and coordinate activities with other ants.
paras.zh: 特别重要的是负责气味受体的基因，它使蚂蚁能够检测气味并做出反应。这些受体对于蚂蚁社会行为的几乎每个方面都至关重要。蚂蚁在很大程度上依赖化学信号来在环境中寻找出路、识别自己蚁群的成员以及与其他蚂蚁协调活动。

paras.en: The findings suggest that jumping genes may have contributed to the expansion of these sensory systems, potentially improving the ability of ants to detect and interpret the chemical messages that make their complex societies possible.
paras.zh: 研究结果表明，跳跃基因可能有助于这些感觉系统的扩展，从而有可能提高蚂蚁检测和解释化学信息的能力，从而使它们的复杂社会成为可能。

paras.en: Tracing 100 Million Years of Ant Evolution
paras.zh: 追踪蚂蚁一亿年的进化

paras.en: To investigate how jumping genes influenced ant evolution, the international research team examined and compared the genomes of 163 ant species. These represented twelve of the 16 ant subfamilies that survive today, providing a broad picture of the genetic diversity found across modern ants.
paras.zh: 为了研究跳跃基因如何影响蚂蚁进化，国际研究小组检查并比较了 163 种蚂蚁的基因组。这些代表了今天幸存的 16 个蚂蚁亚科中的 12 个，提供了现代蚂蚁遗传多样性的广阔图景。

paras.en: Using these genomic comparisons, the scientists reconstructed how transposable elements evolved and changed in activity over the past 100 million years.
paras.zh: 利用这些基因组比较，科学家们重建了转座元件在过去一亿年中如何进化和活动变化。

paras.en: Their results reveal a striking connection between ancient bursts of jumping gene activity and the later diversification of ants, suggesting that DNA sequences once dismissed as genetic parasites may have helped one of Earth's most successful insect groups flourish.
paras.zh: 他们的结果揭示了古代跳跃基因活动的爆发与后来蚂蚁的多样化之间存在惊人的联系，这表明曾经被视为遗传寄生虫的 DNA 序列可能帮助了地球上最成功的昆虫群体之一的繁荣。
