paras.en: A good laptop docking station lets you convert your laptop into a desktop for a comfier experience when you’re working from home, and this compact beauty from Belkin is one of our top picks. GaN technology (gallium nitride semiconductors, a faster, more compact alternative to silicon) lets Belkin pack more ports than you can shake a USB-C cable at, including 96-watt power delivery, three 4K display ports, a gigabit Ethernet port, and more. This deal equals the lowest price we’ve seen.

Learning about the wildlife in your garden can be a lot of fun, and the best smart bird feeders are an ideal way to see which feathered friends are in the area. The thoughtfully designed Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 has a removable 1.5-liter dual-hopper seed reservoir, is easy to clean, and boasts a solar roof to keep the camera charged up. It snaps 8-megapixel photos, captures 4K video, and includes a nifty AI bird-identification feature. We’ve seen it on sale before, but never this low.

articles.title: Anthropic Flags Gas Supply as One of Its Biggest Near-Term Risks
articles.author: Molly Taft

paras.en: Data centers’ reliance on private natural gas plants is a key near-term risk to Anthropic. In the company’s IPO filing on Monday, it warned that the data center gas buildout could drive prices higher in some regions, affecting its AI ambitions and other data center operators around the country.

As America’s data center boom keeps growing, the facilities are set to consume a staggering amount of natural gas, with many companies opting to build their own plants rather than wait years for grid connection. Energy analyst company Cleanview estimates that behind-the-meter gas projects in development as of October 2026 at 110 gigawatts, up from just 20 gigawatts in July of 2025.

Competition from other natural gas-fired data centers could leave Anthropic exposed to “fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control,” the company wrote in its IPO filing, and “could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

The surge in demand for gas comes on top of an already tight market for natural gas. US export terminals are sending more gas abroad for a variety of reasons, including geopolitical conflicts and federal support for exports. Export demand is expected to double over the next decade.

Still, data centers could add a hefty chunk of demand, even if just some of what’s in the pipeline is built. BloombergNEF estimates that grid-connected data centers alone could add an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas demand by 2035, a 15 percent increase in overall demand. Adding on a conservative estimate of onsite gas capacity in the pipeline would add another 3 billion cubic feet per day by the next decade.

Anthropic has traditionally relied on renting compute from major cloud service providers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX are specifically named in the IPO. (Anthropic is renting server space from the latter’s Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee, which is facing a lawsuit for relying on unpermitted gas turbines.)

But the company has moved in recent months to directly lease and develop data centers, in a bid to lessen its reliance on other tech giants and more directly control its own data centers. In the IPO, it singles out its $50 billion partnership with Fluidstack, announced last year, which “provides data center development and operations services” for the company. It has announced data center sites in Texas and New York.

Doing so, though, exposes it to more risks, including the rises in natural gas prices. The company has also been tied to developing data centers with major on-site gas projects in states as spread out as Louisiana, Texas, and West Virginia. The latter could eventually be among the largest gas plants in the US, according to developer Nscale’s own IPO filing.

The geographical dispersion of its data centers opens Anthropic up to regional gas supply shocks and markets. That’s particularly true in the Southeast, where projects will have to compete with LNG exports.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if you start to see gas start to get more expensive in Louisiana and Texas, where all the LNG projects are concentrated,” says Enrique Gonzalez, BNEF’s head of gas research for the Americas.

Texas is also the national hotspot for behind-the-meter data center development, putting multiple developers in competition for the same, potentially limited gas supply. Anthropic acknowledges this risk in its IPO filing, writing that “we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

Any strain on gas supply could have knock-on prices for home energy bills. Gonzalez thinks that natural gas producers learned their lesson from the energy crisis of 2022, when high gas prices caused production to increase, in turn knocking down prices. While markets are unlikely to be that extreme in the coming years, “if hub prices rise, there’s a chance—unless you have legislation—that it goes to consumers,” he says.

One solution for this is, of course, to look at renewables, which also have the added climate benefit of being carbon-free. But Anthropic mentions them once in its IPO filing, and only to dismiss them. “Newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost,” the prospectus states.

articles.title: Watch: Amy Poehler leads archaeological dig in new comedy 'Dig'

paras.en: Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Peacock is giving a glimpse of the new series Dig.
The streaming service shared a trailer for the show Tuesday featuring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie.
Dig hails from Poehler and Michael Schur, the co-creator of Parks and Recreation and creator of The Good Place.

Based on the Kate Myers novel Excavations, the comedy series stars Poehler as Elise, a woman leading an archaeological dig in Greece. Elise and her team discover a mysterious artifact that "sends them on the adventure of a lifetime."
Geraldine Viswanathan, Fina Strazza and Antonia Thomas also star, with Laurie portraying British professor Neville.
Dig consists of 10 episodes and will premiere in its entirety Nov. 23 on Peacock.

articles.title: FBI raids Beverly Hills, Calif., mansion connected to former congressman Eric Swalwell

paras.en: Oct. 27 (UPI) -- The FBI raided the Beverly Hills, Calif., mansion of billionaire Stephen Cloobeck on Tuesday, a mansion that was used for events supporting former Rep. Eric Swalwell's campaign for California governor.

Cloobeck was a supporter of Swalwell's campaign and the former congressman stayed at the home on occasion while campaigning for governor. He ended his campaign after being accused of rape and sexual assault by multiple women.
Cloobeck withdrew his support for Swalwell after the allegations were made public.

Cloobeck, 64, was arrested in May on charges related to attempting to dissuade witnesses from testifying in a case against his fiancée, model and social media influencer Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura.
Lavie was charged in November with eight felonies for allegedly stealing from men she met online, in some cases by burglary.
FBI spokesperson Lourdes Arocho said the FBI was executing a search warrant on Tuesday and no arrests were planned.

Swalwell is the subject of criminal investigations by the Manhattan District Attorney's Office and Los Angeles Sheriff's Department over the allegations of rape and sexual abuse against him. Federal authorities seized electronic devices from Swalwell in August at the San Francisco airport. Devices were also taken from his home in Washington, D.C., as part of an investigation into the allegations against him.

articles.title: Mexico exports jump 38% as trade deficit returns

paras.en: Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Mexico's exports surged 37.9% in September from a year earlier, driven by strong manufacturing and electronics shipments, even as the country recorded a $606 million trade deficit, according to figures released Tuesday by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography.

Exports reached $77.8 billion, the third-highest monthly total on record and the highest for any September, according to Mexican business publication Expansión. Imports climbed 33.1% to $78.4 billion, reversing a $605 million trade surplus recorded in August.

Manufactured goods accounted for most of the growth, with exports rising 39% to $72.8 billion. Shipments of electrical and electronic equipment increased 94.7% from September 2025, while exports of nonautomotive manufactured goods jumped 53%, according to INEGI.

The figures also highlighted Mexico's trade ties with the United States. Non-oil exports to the U.S. market increased 43.5% year over year, compared with a 16.4% rise in shipments to the rest of the world. The Mexican newspaper La Jornada reported that the United States accounted for approximately 84% of Mexico's exports during the first nine months of 2026.

Automotive exports, traditionally one of Mexico's main manufacturing sectors, grew at a slower pace. Shipments rose 5.7% to $16.4 billion, supported by an 8.5% increase in sales to the United States, while exports to other markets declined 7.4%, according to Expansión.

The rapid expansion of electronics exports comes amid growing demand for computers, servers and other equipment used in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers. Mexican financial newspaper El Economista identified computing equipment as a major driver of the increase in nonautomotive manufacturing exports.

Despite September's trade deficit, Mexico maintained a cumulative trade surplus of $9.25 billion during the first nine months of 2026, compared with a $3.4 billion deficit during the same period last year, INEGI reported. Total exports reached $627.2 billion, up 30.4%, while imports increased 27.5% to $617.9 billion.

The September deficit reflected a narrowing surplus in non-oil trade, which fell from $4.05 billion in August to $2.75 billion. Mexico's oil trade deficit also declined silghtly, from $3.44 billion to $3.35 billion, according to the statistics agency.

articles.title: Votes from Israel’s Arab citizens could help decide the election.
articles.author: Natan Odenheimer and Heedo Abu Laban

paras.en: Israelis flocked to the polls in record numbers on Tuesday in what is widely seen as the most consequential election in the country’s history, as voters decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition in power or chart a new course.
paras.zh: 以色列人周二涌向民意调查，人数创下纪录，这被广泛认为是该国历史上最重要的选举，因为选民决定是让总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡(Benjamin Netanyahu)及其极右翼联盟继续掌权，还是制定新的路线。

paras.en: By 6 p.m. local time (12 p.m. Eastern), four hours before polls were scheduled to close, 66.7 percent of voters had cast ballots.
paras.zh: 截至当地时间下午6点（美国东部时间中午12点） ，即投票原定结束前4小时， 66.7%的选民投票。

paras.en: Turnout appeared to be particularly high, compared with previous elections, among Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population. By late afternoon, hours before the polls were set to close, turnout in some Arab-majority towns had exceeded the totals from the last election, in 2022.
paras.zh: 与之前的选举相比，阿拉伯公民的投票率似乎特别高，他们约占以色列人口的五分之一。截至下午晚些时候，在投票结束前的几个小时，一些阿拉伯人占多数的城镇的投票率已经超过了2022年上次选举的总数。

paras.en: Responding to the high turnout in those towns, Mr. Netanyahu accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections,” repeatedly using brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
paras.zh: 针对这些城镇的高投票率，内塔尼亚胡先生指责阿拉伯公民“试图窃取选举” ，一再使用厚颜无耻和公开的种族呼吁来推动他的右翼基础投票。

paras.en: The election is Israel’s first since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, upended the nation and ignited three years of war.
paras.zh: 这次选举是自2023年10月7日哈马斯领导的袭击以来以色列的第一次选举，颠覆了国家并引发了三年的战争。

paras.en: Voters have a choice between two blocs offering starkly different visions. Mr. Netanyahu is seeking re-election at the helm of the most far-right government in Israeli history. His coalition of nationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jews faces an ideologically diverse group of Jewish opposition parties loosely led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff whose son was killed in the Gaza war. Parties representing Arab citizens of Israel also staunchly oppose Mr. Netanyahu’s government.
paras.zh: 选民可以在提供截然不同愿景的两个集团之间做出选择。内塔尼亚胡正在寻求连任以色列历史上最右翼的政府。他的民族主义者和极端正统犹太人联盟面临着一个意识形态多样化的犹太反对党团体，由前军事参谋长加迪·艾森科特（ Gadi Eisenkot ）松散领导，他的儿子在加沙战争中丧生。代表以色列阿拉伯公民的政党也坚决反对内塔尼亚胡政府。

paras.en: Both sides are framing the election as a make-or-break moment for the country. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition offers the promise of a more religious Israel with an ever-tighter grip over the West Bank and Gaza. His opponents are casting the vote as the last chance to preserve democracy and pull Israel back from the brink of becoming a pariah state under international sanctions.
paras.zh: 双方都将选举视为该国的成败时刻。内塔尼亚胡的联盟承诺建立一个更加虔诚的以色列，对约旦河西岸和加沙地带的控制越来越严格。他的反对者将投票作为维护民主和将以色列从国际制裁下的贱民国家边缘拉回来的最后机会。

paras.en: Voting will close at 10 p.m. but is unlikely to deliver an immediate verdict on who will be the next prime minister. Opinion polls suggest that Mr. Netanyahu’s allies and rivals are roughly tied, and assembling a governing coalition in Israel’s parliamentary system could take weeks or months.
paras.zh: 投票将于晚上10点结束，但不太可能立即对谁将成为下一任总理做出裁决。民意调查显示，内塔尼亚胡的盟友和竞争对手大致平起平坐，在以色列议会系统中组建执政联盟可能需要数周或数月时间。

paras.en: Opposition leaders led by Mr. Eisenkot have called for a reckoning over what they call Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to prevent the catastrophic Oct. 7 attacks. They also have pledged to repair Israel’s shattered image abroad, including by cracking down on Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
paras.zh: 以艾森科特为首的反对派领导人呼吁对内塔尼亚胡未能阻止10月7日的灾难性袭击进行清算。他们还承诺修复以色列在国外的破碎形象，包括打击以色列在被占领的约旦河西岸对巴勒斯坦人的极端主义暴力行为。

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu has resisted the establishment of an independent commission to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks. He has vowed to move ahead with overhauling Israel’s judicial system, a move that critics say could undermine the country’s liberal democracy. And his allies say they hope to permanently entrench Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza despite international condemnation.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡抵制成立一个独立委员会来调查10月7日的袭击事件。他发誓要推进以色列司法系统的改革，批评人士认为此举可能会破坏该国的自由民主。他的盟友表示，尽管受到国际谴责，但他们希望永久巩固以色列在约旦河西岸和加沙的统治。

paras.en: The 77-year-old leader has dominated Israeli politics for decades. In recent days, he repeatedly suggested that the country could face annihilation without him in charge.
paras.zh: 这位77岁的领导人几十年来一直主导着以色列的政治。最近几天，他一再暗示，如果没有他，这个国家可能会面临灭绝。

paras.en: - Poll times: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party said it had asked the Central Election Committee to extend voting hours nationally beyond 10 p.m., an unheard-of move that election officials are unlikely to grant. Likud’s rivals argued that the highly unusual request was intended to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.
paras.zh: -投票时间：内塔尼亚胡所在的利库德集团表示，已要求中央选举委员会将全国投票时间延长至晚上10点之后，这是选举官员不太可能同意的史无前例的举动。利库德集团的竞争对手辩称，这一极不寻常的要求旨在对选举的完整性产生怀疑。

paras.en: - Election integrity: Mr. Netanyahu used racially charged language to cast suspicion over high turnout among Arab citizens and to encourage his base to go to the polls. Election officials said Tuesday that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.
paras.zh: -选举诚信：内塔尼亚胡先生使用种族歧视的语言对阿拉伯公民的高投票率表示怀疑，并鼓励他的基地去投票。选举官员周二表示，没有迹象表明存在普遍的违规行为。

paras.en: - Trump weighs in: President Trump has endorsed Mr. Netanyahu, praising him as an important partner in the war against Iran and saying anyone else would be the “wrong leader” for Israel. Analysts were skeptical that the U.S. president’s intervention would sway many voters.
paras.zh: -特朗普权衡：特朗普总统支持内塔尼亚胡，称赞他是对伊朗战争的重要合作伙伴，并称其他任何人都将是以色列的“错误领导人”。分析人士怀疑美国总统的干预会影响许多选民。

paras.en: Turnout data may help explain why Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is worried about the pace of voting. With just over three hours until polls close, turnout in the five towns where his Likud party won its strongest support in 2022 was below the national rate by up to 10 percentage points.
paras.zh: 投票率数据可能有助于解释为什么总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡（ Benjamin Netanyahu ）担心投票速度。距离民意调查结束只有三个多小时的时间，他的利库德党在2022年赢得最强支持的五个城镇的投票率比全国投票率低了10个百分点。

paras.en: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections” on Tuesday, as he repeatedly used brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
paras.zh: 以色列总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡（ Benjamin Netanyahu ）周二指责阿拉伯公民“试图窃取选举” ，因为他多次使用厚颜无耻和公开的种族呼吁来推动他的右翼基础投票。

paras.en: “There are buses heading to the polls and long lines in Arab towns. Meanwhile, right-wing strongholds have yet to wake up!” he said on social media. “If we don’t go vote now, we will find ourselves with a government of Arab parties.”
paras.zh: “阿拉伯城镇有前往投票站的巴士和排长队的巴士。与此同时，右翼据点尚未苏醒！”他在社交媒体上说。“如果我们现在不去投票，我们将发现自己与一个由阿拉伯政党组成的政府站在一起。”

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu has a long track record of appealing to his supporters by invoking the specter of the Arab vote. Arab citizens represent about 20 percent of Israel’s population, but have long complained that they are treated as second-class citizens and subject to discrimination.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡在通过援引阿拉伯选票的幽灵来吸引他的支持者方面有着悠久的记录。阿拉伯公民约占以色列人口的20 ％ ，但长期以来一直抱怨他们被当作二等公民对待并受到歧视。

paras.en: In 2015, Mr. Netanyahu called on right-wing Israelis to vote because “Arabs were heading in droves to the polls.” His comments were widely condemned at home and abroad, including by the Obama administration. Mr. Netanyahu was accused of race-baiting and was forced to issue an apology for the remark.
paras.zh: 2015年，内塔尼亚胡呼吁以色列右翼人士投票，因为“阿拉伯人成群结队地前往投票站。他的言论在国内外都受到了广泛的谴责，包括奥巴马政府。内塔尼亚胡先生被指控进行种族诱饵，并被迫为这一言论道歉。

paras.en: On Tuesday, as initial data showed high turnout in Arab cities and towns, Mr. Netanyahu again used almost the same language to vilify Arab voters in several different statements over the course of the day.
paras.zh: 周二，由于初步数据显示阿拉伯城镇的投票率很高，内塔尼亚胡先生在当天的几次不同声明中再次使用了几乎相同的语言来诋毁阿拉伯选民。

paras.en: “They say their voters are heading to the polls in droves. You too must head to the polls in droves,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement, addressing right-wing voters.
paras.zh: “他们说，他们的选民正成群结队地前往投票站。你们也必须成群结队地前往投票站，”内塔尼亚胡在视频声明中对右翼选民说。

paras.en: Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List alliance of Arab parties, accused Mr. Netanyahu of “inciting against Arab citizens and undermining the legitimacy of our vote.”
paras.zh: 领导阿拉伯政党联合名单联盟的尤瑟夫·贾巴林（ Yousef Jabareen ）指责内塔尼亚胡先生“煽动反对阿拉伯公民并破坏我们投票的合法性”。

paras.en: “I’m telling you: the Arab community knows how to punish you,” Mr. Jabareen said. “Today we’re sending you and your bloodstained government packing.”
paras.zh: Jabareen先生说： “我告诉你：阿拉伯社区知道如何惩罚你。” “今天我们送你和你的血迹斑斑的政府包装。”

paras.en: Arab citizens have tended to vote at lower rates than their Jewish counterparts. But in the run-up to this election, surveys suggested that they would turn out in higher numbers in an effort to vote out Mr. Netanyahu and his far-right allies. In Rahat, a large Bedouin town in southern Israel, turnout just before 5 p.m. was already at 60 percent — matching the town’s final turnout in the previous election.
paras.zh: 阿拉伯公民的投票率往往低于犹太公民。但在这次选举前夕，调查显示，他们将以更高的人数投票给内塔尼亚胡及其极右翼盟友。在以色列南部的一个大型贝都因城镇拉哈特，下午5点之前的投票率已经达到60% ，与上次选举中该镇的最终投票率相当。

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party and some hard-right ministers in his government have also deployed incendiary messaging to appeal to supporters to vote.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡领导的利库德集团及其政府中的一些强硬派部长也部署了煽动性信息，呼吁支持者投票。

paras.en: The Likud party released images suggesting that there had been higher turnout in the Arab city of Rahat than Bat Yam, a Likud stronghold, which it called “a state of emergency.”
paras.zh: 利库德集团发布的图像显示，阿拉伯城市拉哈特的投票率高于利库德集团的据点巴特亚姆，后者被称为“紧急状态”。

paras.en: Another poster showed women in Muslim religious veils with the caption: “Right-wing voters, don’t stay home.”
paras.zh: 另一张海报展示了戴着穆斯林宗教面纱的女性，上面写着： “右翼选民，不要呆在家里。”

paras.en: Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, joined in the prime minister in trying to stoke fears over high Arab turnout. In a video filmed near the entrance of the Arab town of Kufr Qassim in central Israel, he said that Arab voters were heading to the polls “at hitherto never-before-seen rates,” threatening Israel’s Jewish character.
paras.zh: 极右翼国家安全部长伊塔马尔·本-格维尔（ Itamar Ben-Gvir ）与总理一起试图引发对阿拉伯高投票率的担忧。在以色列中部阿拉伯城镇Kufr Qassim入口附近拍摄的一段视频中，他说，阿拉伯选民正“以前所未有的速度”前往投票站，威胁到以色列的犹太人性格。

paras.en: The prime minister also pointed to the arrests of three people suspected of planning to bribe voters for Raam, an Arab Israeli party, on Tuesday. Dean Livne, the acting director of Israel’s central elections committee, told reporters that there were no reports of widespread irregularities.
paras.zh: 总理还指出，周二逮捕了三名涉嫌计划为阿拉伯以色列政党Raam贿赂选民的人。以色列中央选举委员会代理主任迪恩·利夫内（ Dean Livne ）告诉记者，没有关于普遍存在违规行为的报道。

paras.en: Lia Lapidotand Johnatan Reisscontributed reporting.
paras.zh: Lia Lapidotan和Johnatan重新撰写报告。

paras.en: Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.
paras.zh: 在2023年10月7日哈马斯领导的对以色列的袭击中，几名亲属被杀或被扣为人质，他们正在参加周二的选举，这是自袭击事件以来的首次全国性投票，震撼了该国的基础并引发了最长的战争。

paras.en: The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.
paras.zh: 2023年10月的袭击事件笼罩着本周的投票。在以色列历史上未能防止最严重的军事、情报和政策灾难的责任人问题上，存在着尖锐的分歧。

paras.en: About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.
paras.zh: 据以色列当局称，当天约有1200名平民和士兵被杀，约250人被扣为人质前往加沙。哈马斯劫持的许多人质家属在电视采访和全国抗议活动中为亲人竞选时声名鹊起。

paras.en: Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.
paras.zh: 他们中的大多数人呼吁内塔尼亚胡总理对10月7日的失败负责，并优先谈判释放人质，而不是继续战斗。其他人支持内塔尼亚胡的右翼政府，并敦促它继续对哈马斯和以色列的其他敌人施加军事压力。

paras.en: Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:
paras.zh: 来自以色列各政治派别的政党从10月7日家族中招募了候选人。以下是有机会赢得议会席位的一些候选人：

paras.en: Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

paras.en: Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.
paras.zh: 获释人质Eitan Mor的父亲Zvi Mor正在竞选以Bezalel Smotrich为首的极右翼政党宗教犹太复国主义的候选人。在Eitan被囚禁期间，教育家Mor先生创立了一个论坛，反对与哈马斯达成交易的右翼人质和士兵的父母，并推动以色列在军事上击败该组织。

paras.en: Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

paras.en: Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

paras.en: Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”
paras.zh: 塔利·格维利（ Tali Gvili ）与内塔尼亚胡的利库德集团（ Likud ）一道，是警方反恐部队成员兰·格维利（ Ran Gvili ）少校的母亲，他于10月7日在战斗中被枪杀并受重伤，然后被拖入加沙。他的遗体于2026年1月被找回并送回以色列。Gvili和内塔尼亚胡家族已经变得亲密起来，总理参加了Gvili中士的国葬，说： “我们的灵魂与你们的灵魂联系在一起。”

paras.en: Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7. Maj. Shahar Varon, a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”

paras.en: Israel’s Central Elections Committee just announced the latest voting data, which show Israelis are still turning out in large numbers. Voter turnout as of 6 p.m. local time is 66.7 percent, the highest for that hour of the day in decades, according to the committee, and nine percentage points higher than in 2022.

“I voted for an Arab party because this is about our very existence. If I don’t go out and vote, I won’t have representation in the Knesset, and I won’t have a presence as an Arab citizen living in this country.”
Sara Abu Sayum, 24, an Arab citizen of Israel who voted in the city of Lod.

For decades, Israel had virtually unanimous support among Republicans and Democrats in Congress, a reflection of a broader consensus in the United States in favor of strong backing for the Jewish state.

But that consensus began to fray several years ago and has recently threatened to unravel altogether as Democrats have shifted drastically and rapidly from unequivocal support for Israel, reflecting a sea change in Americans’ views.

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed, a growing number of Democrats have been under pressure from younger and progressive voters who are a crucial part of their base.

Lawmakers have begun rebuking Israel in ways that were once unimaginable. They have pointed to tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians killed in Gaza and focused much of their ire on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, whose actions and policies have left his country diplomatically isolated and who has become a political lightning rod in the United States. That has put at risk the bipartisan support for military aid that Israel has always counted on from American lawmakers.

A handful of far-right Republicans and libertarians in Congress have also questioned U.S. support for Israel, raising concern about Palestinian deaths and spending American money to defend a far-off ally. But the skepticism is far more widespread among Democrats.

The midterm elections have been shaped in part by Democratic voters’ mounting hostility toward Israel. Party leaders now view the issue as one of the major fault lines they will have to contend with next year if they win back control of Congress in November.

Over the past year, almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off aid to Israel. Democratic leaders who have long been staunch allies have said that the U.S.-Israeli relationship needs a fundamental reset, including a rethinking of the 10-year memorandum of understanding that commits billions of dollars of annual security aid to Israel, which will soon expire.

And Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, who is the highest-ranking Jewish official in the nation, has condemned Mr. Netanyahu on the Senate floor and called for new leadership in Israel.

In recent weeks, top Democrats in the House and the Senate have proposed legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for building settlements, making clear to Israeli companies and banks that they could be penalized for ties to such activity.
Those moves are in line with what lawmakers are hearing from voters.

A New York Times/Siena national poll conducted in May found that 74 percent of Democratic voters opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel. A Pew Research Center poll in April found that eight in 10 Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents had an unfavorable view of Israel.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had asked Israel’s Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past the scheduled closing time of 10 p.m. The committee has the authority to do so, though it would be a highly unusual move.

Netanyahu has repeatedly urged his supporters to head to the polls, saying that right-wing strongholds are failing to turn out in sufficient numbers. The party of Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s leading opponent, said it strongly opposed an extension, arguing that Likud made the request in order to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.

In the run-up to Tuesday’s election Israel, perhaps the country’s most intensely scrutinized vote ever, the authorities and civil society groups mobilized to monitor the balloting, which many fear could be undermined by political interference and disinformation.

In an office building north of Tel Aviv, dozens of volunteer tech workers and lawyers planned to squeeze into a “war room” to field reports from thousands of volunteers watching polling sites for violence or obstruction. The effort is organized by antigovernment protest groups that say their goal is not to encourage voting for any political party but to ensure safe access to polls.

In Jerusalem, officials from the Central Election Committee are overseeing an extensive Election Day operation from Parliament. Committee employees are fanning out to more than 12,000 polling stations wearing body cameras to document irregularities. A desk operated jointly with Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, is scanning the web for disinformation to respond to it in real time.
“This election is the most threatened ever,” said Assaf Shapira, a researcher at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. “The stakes are very high,” he said.

Some experts point to concerns, including the growing sophistication and prevalence of A.I.-generated content, a police force that critics say is increasingly loyal to the far-right minister overseeing it and a sitting Israeli government whose senior officials have repeatedly suggested the vote could be rigged.

The Central Election Committee, a partly political body chaired by a Supreme Court justice and whose administrative branch is composed of nonpartisan officials, is working to bolster confidence in the process and counter false claims of fraud, Dean Livne, the committee’s acting director general, said in an interview.

Tallies from each polling station will be made public within hours of the polls closing, and the counting of roughly 600,000 ballots cast remotely at places like hospitals, embassies, and military bases will be live streamed for nearly 24 hours, according to Mr. Livne.
“This election will be the most transparent ever,” he said.

Election observers agree that the risk of widespread fraud or manipulation of the vote count is exceedingly low. And as of Tuesday afternoon, election officials said there had been no indication of widespread irregularities. But some experts also say that government officials could be laying the groundwork to undermine confidence in the election so that they can then challenge an unfavorable result as rigged.

Throughout the campaign, members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party have questioned the impartiality and qualifications of election officials and suggested that antigovernment groups were plotting to obstruct the vote.
“To challenge the legitimacy of elections, you have to plant the seeds early on,” Yael Shomer, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University, said. “And I think we see them planting the seeds.”

Senior government officials have stopped short of explicitly threatening to reject the election result. Mr. Netanyahu recently said that he would stand to lose the election if too few of his supporters turned out to vote.
Observers warn of disinformation campaigns and attempts to intimidate some voters and deter them from casting their ballots on Election Day.

Such attempts, opposition figures and some experts worry, could involve the Israeli police, which is increasingly seen as serving the interests of the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir. Some fear that on Election Day, officers could look the other way at pro-government violence or attempts to intimidate voters outside polling stations in areas considered hostile to Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Ben-Gvir.
Israel’s police commissioner, Danny Levy, has vowed to defend the integrity of the vote and said he would dismiss officers who express political views while on duty.

Concerns about voter intimidation are particularly high for Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up roughly 20 percent of the population and typically vote for parties opposed to Mr. Netanyahu’s. Turnout in Arab communities has historically been low, and they have been targeted with largely unsubstantiated allegations of widespread voter fraud by Mr. Netanyahu and his political allies.

Earlier this month, Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, announced plans to deploy thousands of religious Jewish “observers” to “prevent fraud in voting and vote-counting in Arab communities.” Critics fear that could instigate chaos and discourage Arab citizens from going out to vote.

Officials in Arab localities are organizing teams to share verified information with their communities to combat disinformation intended to deter voting, including false reports of polling station closures or violence around voting sites, said Abed Shahada, who leads an effort to increase turnout for an organization representing Arab local officials.
“The threats are greater, but there is also a greater awareness of them,” he said. “We’re trying to have one confront the other.”

One noticeable trend is strong turnout in some of Israel’s largest Arab-majority towns. In Rahat, a Bedouin town in southern Israel, turnout stood at 60 percent just before 5 p.m. That was the town’s final turnout in the previous election once polls closed at 10 p.m. In Nazareth, it was roughly 46 percent, two percentage points below its final turnout in 2022.
I’m in Har Nof, an ultra-Orthodox neighborhood in Jerusalem, which is a stronghold of the Shas party that has long been in a tight political alliance with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Israelis are continuing to vote in large numbers, reflecting how many have said the election is a turning point for the country. More than 55 percent have voted as of 4 p.m. local time, the largest tally at that hour since the elections committee began tracking incremental turnout in the 1970s.
“Bibi flows in my blood. No one can replace Bibi. He’s strong, a world leader.”
Shoshi Ashtbeker, 47, a school secretary from Tel Aviv, referring to Benjamin Netanyahu, whom she said she’d voted for all her life.
Arab voters could tip the scales as Israelis turned out in large numbers to vote on Tuesday in one of their country’s most consequential elections in decades.

Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population, have historically voted at significantly lower rates than Jewish Israelis in national elections. But pollsters, researchers and activists expected Arab voters to turn out in force, driven to unseat a right-wing government that has enacted aggressive policies against them.

Arab Israelis are overwhelmingly Muslim, with Druse and Christian communities making up around 15 percent. Palestinians living in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are not Israeli citizens and cannot vote.

Recent polls suggest that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing alliance nor the opposition bloc is likely to form a majority without a partnership with Arab parties. Such a stalemate would leave Arab leaders with huge influence on the results.

“The stakes are too high to sit this one out,” said Sireen Jabareen, 30, a director of a rights organization that helps Arab prisoners. She said she would vote for the first time after previously boycotting the political system, which she views as discriminatory toward Arabs. “I don’t want to be the kind of person who clings to rigid principles when reality changes,” she added.

Many others have also stayed home on Election Day in the past, alienated by political leaders, convinced their ballots hold no sway or unwilling to validate a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens.

Arab politicians and local leaders are warning of voter-suppression efforts, through either disinformation campaigns or the presence of armed right-wing activists near polling stations in Arab villages.

Last week, Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party announced a joint effort with another right-wing party to send 2,000 activists to oversee “voting integrity” in Arab cities and towns. The move was widely seen as an attempt to suppress Arab voters.

In the 2015 election, Mr. Netanyahu sought to prod supporters by saying that Arab voters were “heading to the polls in huge quantities.” After critics accused him of race-baiting, he apologized for any offense caused by the remark.

But on Tuesday, he tried a similar tactic, pointing to apparently high turnout among Arab voters and suggesting that they were “trying to steal the elections.” (Election authorities said there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.) Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party released a poster showing a crowd of women in hijab, urging right-wing Israelis “not to stay home.”

Yousef Makladeh, a leading pollster focusing on Arab society in Israel, said recent surveys indicated that 65 percent to 70 percent of Arab voters planned to vote on Tuesday. That would be an increase of 12 to 18 percentage points over turnout in the 2022 election.
For the very first time, activists say, efforts to turn out the vote feel like pushing on an open door.

Omar Abu Siyam, a social media personality from Mu’awiya, an Arab village near Haifa, Israel, said that when he told his nearly 90,000 Instagram followers that he had changed his mind and decided to vote, hundreds of commenters responded that they felt the same way.

The most critical issue for Arab voters by a wide margin, Mr. Makladeh said, is the surge in violent crime within their communities, a crisis many say the police have deliberately neglected under Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister.

“Arabs are terrified of what four more years with Ben-Gvir in office will do to us,” said Dr. Thabet Abu Ras, a political geographer who is advising voter-turnout initiatives across Arab municipalities. He added that discriminatory housing policies, resulting in a record number of home demolitions in Arab communities, were also driving voters.

Higher Arab turnout could threaten smaller parties that are more likely to support Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition. By increasing the total number of votes cast, it would raise the threshold for smaller parties to win seats in the Knesset.
“This time,” Dr. Abu Ras said, “the Arab vote is worth gold.”

The latest update from Israel’s Central Elections Committee said that as of 2 p.m. local time, voter turnout was 44.9 percent — the highest in decades for that time of day and six percentage points more than at the same point in the 2022 general election. Dean Livne, the committee’s acting director, told reporters that there were still long lines at some polling places. Anyone who is waiting in line at 10 p.m., when the polls close, will be allowed to cast a vote, he said.
Israelis voting on Tuesday will encounter a smorgasbord of ballot slips printed with the initials and names of no less than 36 parties in the election.

The majority have no chance of making it into the 120-seat Parliament — but a quirk of the Israeli election system ensures that even the most obscure contenders get their moment in the political limelight.

While parties are barred from buying television time in Israel, they are entitled to seven minutes of free airtime on each of the main television and radio channels — with extra time for every seat that a party holds in the outgoing Parliament. Nightly blocks of election broadcasts, which can run for almost an hour in the two weeks before the ballot, have been a mainstay of campaigns since television arrived here in the 1960s.
The campaign features about a dozen larger parties that are expected to meet, or come close to, the four-seat minimum threshold to enter Parliament.

But every Israeli election also includes an array of esoteric parties run by a gamut of characters from would-be messiahs to pranksters. Of the 38 parties that registered with Israel’s Central Elections Committee, two have since dropped out.

The Pirate Party of Israel has been running in Israeli elections since 2012 on a platform that calls for civil liberties in the digital age as well as free internet and “peace between all the people who live here.” For this election, the party has Dan Ariely — an Israeli American behavioral economist and best-selling author — running in the third slot of its optimistically expansive 24-person slate of candidates.

Another party, Sharshar for Love and Unity, is led by Eitan Shvili, who cosplays a monarch called King Sharshar in full royal regalia complete with a bejeweled crown and a blue cape. His bid for the premiership, clearly a long shot, comes with a promise of a free theater ticket for every Israeli adult.

Gan Eden, or Paradise, party wants to build a society based on peace, justice, freedom and plenty. The party has called for reforming the education system to better connect it with spirituality, removing taxes on basic goods and also promoting dialogue between Jews, Muslims, Christians and other communities — a worthy cause but not one that is likely to carry this party of relative unknowns into the Parliament.

There’s also the Everlasting Covenant for the Salvation of Israel party, which calls for a constitution based on the Torah; and the Bible Bloc, a Jewish-Christian party whose leader, Avi Dennis Lipkin, warns from his living room that Israel must prepare to take in 10 million Jews and non-Jews because of an impending holocaust abroad.

And in what could be seen as a cynical use of the democratic process, the wife and the mother of the Israeli extremist who assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 are leading a party calling for his release from prison. The assassin, Yigal Amir, is serving a life sentence. Israel passed a law in 2001 barring the commutation of a sentence of anyone convicted of assassinating a prime minister, ensuring that Mr. Amir would not be paroled.

Tel Aviv has long been a stronghold for the center left, but I’m in a politically diverse part of town where voters have in previous elections been more evenly divided between support for Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition and the opposition.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, joined the list of top candidates to cast their ballots on Tuesday. He voted in Herzliya, a northern suburb of Tel Aviv, his party’s spokesman said.
Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has been urging his right-wing base to vote by pointing to high turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, suggesting they were “trying to steal the elections.”

The Central Elections Committee told reporters earlier on Tuesday that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities, although the police did arrest three people suspected of attempting to bribe voters to support the Islamist Raam party.
Netanyahu’s Likud party is pushing the same narrative. It released a poster with a crowd of women in hijab, urging right-wing Israelis “not to stay home.”

Netanyahu tried a similar tactic in 2015, prodding supporters with the line that Arab voters were “heading to the polls in huge quantities.” Critics accused him of race baiting. He later apologized for any offense caused by the remark.
On Tuesday, he repeated effectively the same slogan.
“Netanyahu did a lot of big things, but I think he’s done his job. He’s had 20 years in this chair. He can go now.”
Ayelet Veprinskiy, 25, a student in Jerusalem, who said she voted for Naftali Bennett’s Together party.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff for Israel’s military, will likely get the most votes of those hoping to succeed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a pivotal national election on Tuesday.
But that doesn’t mean that only Mr. Eisenkot could lead a government that unseats the longtime leader.

Depending on how Israel’s complex coalition-building process shakes out, at least two other veteran politicians could also find themselves vying for the prime minister’s chair: Avigdor Liberman, a hard-right former defense minister, and Naftali Bennett, a onetime prime minister who has fiercely argued in favor of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Opinion polls in recent months have suggested that Mr. Bennett’s party will secure around a dozen seats in Israel’s 120-member Parliament, or Knesset, while Mr. Liberman’s will collect closer to eight. (Mr. Eisenkot’s party could rack up over 20 seats, according to pre-election polls.)

The political evolutions of Mr. Bennett and Mr. Liberman offer a case study in how Mr. Netanyahu has polarized Israel during his long tenure. The two men should be ideal political partners with the prime minister, as they share many of his hawkish views. Both have worked as advisers to Mr. Netanyahu in the past and even campaigned on his behalf.

Yet they have long since broken with the Israeli leader, and now accuse him of corruption, abuses of power and a willingness to cut deals with extremists in order to remain in charge. Mr. Netanyahu is currently on trial for corruption in three separate but interlocking cases; he has denied all wrongdoing.

A veteran of Israeli politics, Mr. Liberman was born in the Soviet Union and leads the right-wing Yisrael Beitenu party. His base is among the hundreds of thousands of Russian-speaking Jews who similarly emigrated to Israel from the former Communist bloc.

Mr. Liberman lives in the West Bank settlement of Nokdim, and takes a hard-line view on security issues. At one point during the war in Gaza, Mr. Liberman called for Israel to halt all aid, including water, to Palestinians there, even as the enclave faced a humanitarian crisis.

Mr. Bennett served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, during the sole hiatus in Mr. Netanyahu’s premiership since 2009. Though his party secured only seven seats in Parliament in the preceding election, Mr. Bennett leveraged the opposition’s desire to unseat Mr. Netanyahu and he went from being kingmaker to king.

In office, however, Mr. Bennett presided over a fragile, ideologically discordant coalition that ranged from his right-wing Yamina party to Raam, an Islamist party of Arab citizens of Israel. Many of his voters saw his decision to join with left-wing and Arab parties as a betrayal, and as some of his own lawmakers defected, his government collapsed.

Now, Mr. Bennett is running in alliance with Yair Lapid, a centrist who succeeded him as prime minister in the anti-Netanyahu government. In addition to holding large campaign rallies, Mr. Bennett has released videos of himself holding lengthy, impromptu debates with right-wing voters in the streets and around cafe and restaurant tables.
In this election, both Mr. Liberman and Mr. Bennett have focused much of their campaign messaging on Israel’s ultra-Orthodox minority.

The ultra-Orthodox population is 14 percent of Israel’s total but growing rapidly, and they receive far more state benefits than they contribute in taxes, thanks largely to Mr. Netanyahu, who has relied on their support to stay in power.

Ultra-Orthodox religious students are also largely exempt from mandatory military service. During the war in Gaza, religious and secular Israelis alike were furious at what they saw as a powerful minority shirking the wartime burden.
Mr. Bennett has promised to end what he calls an ultra-Orthodox “state within a state” and compel them to participate in national service.

Mr. Liberman, for his part, has inveighed against what he calls an ultra-Orthodox political push for “us to send our children to the army, to do reserve duty, to work, and pay taxes, while they build their own state.” He has accused them of “trying to dismantle the country.”

Turnout continues to look strong. About 31.5 percent of potential voters had cast ballots as of noon, the most by that time of day in an Israeli election since the 1970s, according to Dean Livne, acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee. In 2022, when an election returned Benjamin Netanyahu to power, turnout at 12 p.m. stood at 28.4 percent, according to the committee. Livne told reporters that long lines had been reported at some polling places and urged voters to be patient.

paras.en: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel has led the country’s most right-wing government in recent years, with two ultranationalist ministers in particular pushing policies and positions that have exacerbated friction with many of the nation’s traditional allies.

These politicians, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, who is also responsible for the administration of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, are vocal about expanding Jewish settlements on land that much of the international community considers illegally occupied and designated for a Palestinian state.
But they are not in the same political party or always on the same page. In this election, they are not running on the same slate, unlike in the two previous votes.

Mr. Ben-Gvir leads Otzma Yehudit, or the Jewish Power party; and Mr. Smotrich heads the Religious Zionist party. Mr. Smotrich’s party is running this year on a list with the Zehut, or Identity party, led by Moshe Feiglin, a former member of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party.

Mr. Ben-Gvir has refused Mr. Netanyahu’s attempts to team him and Mr. Smotrich again in hopes of ensuring the parties clear the threshold of 3.25 percent of votes in Israel’s proportional parliamentary system so that the right-wing bloc does not lose any votes. Mr. Smotrich had expressed reservations, as well.

Polling shows Mr. Ben-Gvir is popular with young voters, and he is betting he can secure more parliamentary seats for his party and exercise more power in negotiations to form a right-wing government after the election. He told Time magazine on Thursday that he, nevertheless, supports Mr. Netanyahu and aims to push the next government further right.

Mr. Ben-Gvir is so virulently nationalist that he was not drafted for the Israeli military in his youth. His views were long considered fringe even by other right-wing politicians, like those in Mr. Smotrich’s party.

In recent years, both ministers have gained power domestically and have become known internationally for inflammatory stances and actions. After the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which ignited a devastating war in Gaza, both called for Israel to adopt destructive policies to encourage the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians.

Amid the war, violence by extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank spiked drastically, and both ministers were accused of encouraging impunity. Last year, Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway imposed sanctions on Mr. Ben-Gvir and Mr. Smotrich for “repeated incitements of violence against Palestinian communities.”

Israel has in recent years undertaken an unbridled expansion of Jewish settlements while military operations in the West Bank have resulted in the biggest displacement of Palestinian civilians in the territory since the Arab-Israeli war of 1967. Both Mr. Smotrich and Mr. Ben Gvir want to accelerate these efforts.

Mr. Smotrich has pushed measures extending Israel’s footprint in the West Bank. This year, the security cabinet made it easier for Jews to buy land in parts of the West Bank, and Mr. Smotrich was explicit about his intent. “We are deepening our roots in all parts of the Land of Israel and burying the idea of a Palestinian state,” he said.

In the election, Mr. Netanyahu faces competition from former military general Ofer Winter, who formed a new right-wing party, People of Israel. Recent polling shows the party is drawing support from Likud even as the opposition presents a significant challenge.
And Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the war in Gaza, is the leading candidate against Mr. Netanyahu.

Israelis don’t vote for a prime minister individually, but for a list of candidates presented by a party or parties. The premiership does not automatically go to the party with the most votes, and much more wrangling is needed before it becomes clear who the next leader will be.

Last year, Mr. Eisenkot formed the party Yashar! — Hebrew for “straight” or “honest” — and has said that he will not serve on a government with Mr. Netanyahu. He says he is running to “save Israel” from endless wars and policies dividing Israelis and destroying its international standing, as well as from Mr. Netanyahu. Polling in the days ahead of the election shows Mr. Eisenkot’s party with a slight lead over Likud, potentially securing more seats in the Knesset, or Parliament, than the prime minister’s party.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But the Israeli electoral system is complicated and no party has ever won a majority of seats in the Knesset, so there has been much debate and deal-making to build potential future governing coalitions ahead of the vote, and they will continue after the results are in.

The Henrietta Szold school in the Rehavia section of Jerusalem, which Benjamin Netanyahu attended as a child, is a polling station. Nearby, the streets are plastered with campaign signs and volunteers are out electioneering in force.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, have emerged as the top candidates to form the next government in Israel after the general election on Tuesday, the country’s first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks set off the war in Gaza.
But other candidates have brought their own drama to the campaign, which has also featured revelations about security failures and a furor over an A.I.-generated political ad.
Here are some key moments from the campaign.

Before Election Day had even been set, the opposition politicians Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, both former prime ministers, announced a joint run for office. The two men have worked together before: They briefly unseated Mr. Netanyahu in 2021, forming a government that lasted less than two years.

Their announcement in April was seen as mutually beneficial, positioning Mr. Bennett as a candidate for prime minister and ensuring that Mr. Lapid would remain one of the most prominent figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc.
But their ambition to make their unified party, B’Yachad, the largest in the Knesset quickly fizzled. Surveys consistently suggest the party will finish in third place.

Parties across Israel’s political spectrum have published A.I.-generated content to reinforce their messaging. The content has sometimes stirred up controversy — no more so than in July, when Mr. Netanyahu posted a video depicting Mr. Eisenkot.

In the video, Mr. Eisenkot is shown running through a meadow, arms open, toward a man with a striking resemblance to his late son Gal, who was killed in 2023 at the start of the Israeli military’s war in Gaza. But he runs past the young man, instead embracing Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab politician. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to paint Mr. Abbas, who could help Mr. Eisenkot form a governing coalition, as a supporter of terrorism.

Mr. Netanyahu’s party, Likud, denied that the young man in the video looked like Mr. Eisenkot’s son or was meant to evoke him. But many Israelis reacted to the ad with anger and disgust. Matan Kahana, a former lawmaker running on Mr. Eisenkot’s slate, said there was “no bottom to the pit the Likud is willing to sink into.”

One of the campaign’s most surprising moments came when Mr. Abbas and Yoav Segalovitz, a veteran Zionist politician and former police commander, announced a joint run. Teaming up on the slate of the United Arab List, or Raam, they offered themselves as an example of Jewish-Arab cooperation, even as they braced for intense criticism from both of their communities.

“There are people who are afraid of partnership,” Mr. Abbas said. “There are parties that are afraid of partnership. They are afraid of what people will say, afraid of what they will lose. Raam is not afraid of partnership. Raam advances it.”

Mr. Netanyahu came under new pressure over reports in the Israeli media and in The New York Times that Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed, the president of the United Arab Emirates, had warned him in advance of Oct. 7, 2023, that Hamas was considering a major attack on Israel.
The warning from Sheikh Mohammed never reached the leaders of Israel’s security establishment, The Times reported, citing five former senior Israeli officials. Mr. Netanyahu has denied the reports.

Israelis seemed to forget the election for a day in late September, when the news emerged that a handful of their fellow citizens had stopped a pilot from crashing a FlyDubai commercial jet bound for Tel Aviv.
Mr. Netanyahu spent hours celebrating the passengers’ resourcefulness, diverting attention away from headlines at the time about his and other officials’ failure to stop the Hamas-led attack in 2023.

Within days, however, his government was on the defensive over revelations of security failures that had allowed the FlyDubai pilot, an Omani man said to have embraced extreme Islamist views, into the cockpit in the first place.

Initial signs are that voter turnout is strong. As of 10 a.m., three hours after polls opened, turnout was 16.7 percent, compared to 15.9 percent at the same point in the last general election, in 2022, according to the Central Elections Committee.

Four years of internal turmoil, war and growing global isolation have left Israelis bitterly divided over their country’s future as they vote in national elections on Tuesday. Opinion polls suggest it will be a close race with the possibility that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party nor his opponents will secure a majority.

Many Israelis see the election as a choice over whether to continue the rule of the country’s most hard-line, right-wing government ever, and the dominant fault line is Mr. Netanyahu himself. Critics say he has steered Israel to the lowest point in its history, while his supporters see him as an indispensable leader who has tried to destroy Israel’s enemies in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Beyond Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership, however, there are plenty of issues polarizing the country.

The Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, loom over the vote. About 1,200 Israelis were killed in the assault and 250 were seized as hostages, according to the Israeli authorities, making it the deadliest day in Israeli history.

Israel’s military response in Gaza leveled much of the enclave and killed more than 70,000 people, according to local officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants. Most of the enclave’s two million residents were displaced, often multiple times.

Three years later, Israelis still have no official answer about why Mr. Netanyahu’s government and the Israeli military failed to foresee the attacks and then struggled to respond even as Hamas fighters invaded villages and a music festival, killing civilians.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents — a bloc of opposition parties and their leaders — have said they would establish an independent inquiry with broad authority, appointed by the president of the Supreme Court. Mr. Netanyahu has called for a “democratic and equitable” commission that would be made of an equal number of representatives of the coalition and the opposition.
Families of those killed and taken hostage broadly back the opposition, arguing that Mr. Netanyahu’s proposal would politicize what should be a comprehensive and dispassionate investigation.

Secular and liberal Israelis have long been uneasy about the status of the ultra-Orthodox, an insular community that adheres to a fundamentalist interpretation of Jewish scripture and makes up roughly 14 percent of the population. Their religious students are eligible for an exemption from mandatory military service and receive state benefits despite not joining the work force.

During the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, that long-simmering frustration boiled over into outrage. Hundreds of Israelis from other backgrounds were killed in combat, and hundreds of thousands more did dangerous rounds of reserve duty.

Mr. Netanyahu’s government has relied heavily on the support of ultra-Orthodox parties. His opponents have called for ending the exemption to the draft for the ultra-Orthodox and cutting off welfare benefits for those who avoid military service.

Before the war, Mr. Netanyahu’s government had sought to advance a highly contentious plan to weaken Israel’s judiciary. Critics, including the president of Israel’s Supreme Court, argued that it would fundamentally undermine Israeli democracy.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested the proposals in mass demonstrations, saying that Mr. Netanyahu was leading the country toward dictatorship.

The Hamas-led attacks largely suspended the overhaul, part of which was also reversed by a Supreme Court ruling. But Mr. Netanyahu’s allies say they will push ahead with the changes if they are re-elected.

While global attention has focused on the West Bank and Gaza, domestically both Mr. Netanyahu and his opponents have preferred to focus elsewhere. Mr. Netanyahu and most of his leading rivals say they oppose giving the Palestinians an independent state.
They still offer different visions for the near future.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition is dominated by religious nationalists who have advanced Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank at a breakneck pace. They have called for Israel to urge Palestinians to leave Gaza, with one senior minister saying conditions there should be kept miserable to “take away their hope.”

The fractious bloc of parties opposing Mr. Netanyahu hold wildly diverging views on the Palestinians. They include the left-wing Democrats party, whose members generally support a two-state solution but would have limited influence in a future coalition.

Gadi Eisenkot, who opinion polls suggest will lead the alliance, has vowed to rein in Israeli extremist attacks on Palestinians and engage on the Trump administration’s cease-fire plan for Gaza. But Mr. Eisenkot also supports some Israeli settlements in the West Bank and has even attacked Mr. Netanyahu for having once supported a Palestinian state.

articles.title: Netanyahu accuses Arab citizens of ‘trying to steal the elections’ in racial appeal to voters.
articles.author: Aaron Boxerman

paras.en: Israelis flocked to the polls in record numbers on Tuesday in what is widely seen as the most consequential election in the country’s history, as voters decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition in power or chart a new course.
paras.zh: 以色列人周二涌向民意调查，人数创下纪录，这被广泛认为是该国历史上最重要的选举，因为选民决定是让总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡(Benjamin Netanyahu)及其极右翼联盟继续掌权，还是制定新的路线。

paras.en: By 6 p.m. local time (12 p.m. Eastern), four hours before polls were scheduled to close, 66.7 percent of voters had cast ballots.
paras.zh: 截至当地时间下午6点（美国东部时间中午12点） ，即投票原定结束前4小时， 66.7%的选民投票。

paras.en: Turnout appeared to be particularly high, compared with previous elections, among Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population. By late afternoon, hours before the polls were set to close, turnout in some Arab-majority towns had exceeded the totals from the last election, in 2022.
paras.zh: 与之前的选举相比，阿拉伯公民的投票率似乎特别高，他们约占以色列人口的五分之一。截至下午晚些时候，在投票结束前的几个小时，一些阿拉伯人占多数的城镇的投票率已经超过了2022年上次选举的总数。

paras.en: Responding to the high turnout in those towns, Mr. Netanyahu accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections,” repeatedly using brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
paras.zh: 针对这些城镇的高投票率，内塔尼亚胡先生指责阿拉伯公民“试图窃取选举” ，一再使用厚颜无耻和公开的种族呼吁来推动他的右翼基础投票。

paras.en: The election is Israel’s first since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, upended the nation and ignited three years of war.
paras.zh: 这次选举是自2023年10月7日哈马斯领导的袭击以来以色列的第一次选举，颠覆了国家并引发了三年的战争。

paras.en: Voters have a choice between two blocs offering starkly different visions. Mr. Netanyahu is seeking re-election at the helm of the most far-right government in Israeli history. His coalition of nationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jews faces an ideologically diverse group of Jewish opposition parties loosely led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff whose son was killed in the Gaza war. Parties representing Arab citizens of Israel also staunchly oppose Mr. Netanyahu’s government.
paras.zh: 选民可以在提供截然不同愿景的两个集团之间做出选择。内塔尼亚胡正在寻求连任以色列历史上最右翼的政府。他的民族主义者和极端正统犹太人联盟面临着一个意识形态多样化的犹太反对党团体，由前军事参谋长加迪·艾森科特（ Gadi Eisenkot ）松散领导，他的儿子在加沙战争中丧生。代表以色列阿拉伯公民的政党也坚决反对内塔尼亚胡政府。

paras.en: Both sides are framing the election as a make-or-break moment for the country. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition offers the promise of a more religious Israel with an ever-tighter grip over the West Bank and Gaza. His opponents are casting the vote as the last chance to preserve democracy and pull Israel back from the brink of becoming a pariah state under international sanctions.
paras.zh: 双方都将选举视为该国的成败时刻。内塔尼亚胡的联盟承诺建立一个更加虔诚的以色列，对约旦河西岸和加沙地带的控制越来越严格。他的反对者将投票作为维护民主和将以色列从国际制裁下的贱民国家边缘拉回来的最后机会。

paras.en: Voting will close at 10 p.m. but is unlikely to deliver an immediate verdict on who will be the next prime minister. Opinion polls suggest that Mr. Netanyahu’s allies and rivals are roughly tied, and assembling a governing coalition in Israel’s parliamentary system could take weeks or months.
paras.zh: 投票将于晚上10点结束，但不太可能立即对谁将成为下一任总理做出裁决。民意调查显示，内塔尼亚胡的盟友和竞争对手大致平起平坐，在以色列议会系统中组建执政联盟可能需要数周或数月时间。

paras.en: Opposition leaders led by Mr. Eisenkot have called for a reckoning over what they call Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to prevent the catastrophic Oct. 7 attacks. They also have pledged to repair Israel’s shattered image abroad, including by cracking down on Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
paras.zh: 以艾森科特为首的反对派领导人呼吁对内塔尼亚胡未能阻止10月7日的灾难性袭击进行清算。他们还承诺修复以色列在国外的破碎形象，包括打击以色列在被占领的约旦河西岸对巴勒斯坦人的极端主义暴力行为。

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu has resisted the establishment of an independent commission to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks. He has vowed to move ahead with overhauling Israel’s judicial system, a move that critics say could undermine the country’s liberal democracy. And his allies say they hope to permanently entrench Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza despite international condemnation.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡抵制成立一个独立委员会来调查10月7日的袭击事件。他发誓要推进以色列司法系统的改革，批评人士认为此举可能会破坏该国的自由民主。他的盟友表示，尽管受到国际谴责，但他们希望永久巩固以色列在约旦河西岸和加沙的统治。

paras.en: The 77-year-old leader has dominated Israeli politics for decades. In recent days, he repeatedly suggested that the country could face annihilation without him in charge.
paras.zh: 这位77岁的领导人几十年来一直主导着以色列的政治。最近几天，他一再暗示，如果没有他，这个国家可能会面临灭绝。

paras.en: - Poll times: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party said it had asked the Central Election Committee to extend voting hours nationally beyond 10 p.m., an unheard-of move that election officials are unlikely to grant. Likud’s rivals argued that the highly unusual request was intended to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.
paras.zh: -投票时间：内塔尼亚胡所在的利库德集团表示，已要求中央选举委员会将全国投票时间延长至晚上10点之后，这是选举官员不太可能同意的史无前例的举动。利库德集团的竞争对手辩称，这一极不寻常的要求旨在对选举的完整性产生怀疑。

paras.en: - Election integrity: Mr. Netanyahu used racially charged language to cast suspicion over high turnout among Arab citizens and to encourage his base to go to the polls. Election officials said Tuesday that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.
paras.zh: -选举诚信：内塔尼亚胡先生使用种族歧视的语言对阿拉伯公民的高投票率表示怀疑，并鼓励他的基地去投票。选举官员周二表示，没有迹象表明存在普遍的违规行为。

paras.en: - Trump weighs in: President Trump has endorsed Mr. Netanyahu, praising him as an important partner in the war against Iran and saying anyone else would be the “wrong leader” for Israel. Analysts were skeptical that the U.S. president’s intervention would sway many voters.
paras.zh: -特朗普权衡：特朗普总统支持内塔尼亚胡，称赞他是对伊朗战争的重要合作伙伴，并称其他任何人都将是以色列的“错误领导人”。分析人士怀疑美国总统的干预会影响许多选民。

paras.en: Turnout data may help explain why Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is worried about the pace of voting. With just over three hours until polls close, turnout in the five towns where his Likud party won its strongest support in 2022 was below the national rate by up to 10 percentage points.
paras.zh: 投票率数据可能有助于解释为什么总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡（ Benjamin Netanyahu ）担心投票速度。距离民意调查结束只有三个多小时的时间，他的利库德党在2022年赢得最强支持的五个城镇的投票率比全国投票率低了10个百分点。

paras.en: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections” on Tuesday, as he repeatedly used brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
paras.zh: 以色列总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡（ Benjamin Netanyahu ）周二指责阿拉伯公民“试图窃取选举” ，因为他多次使用厚颜无耻和公开的种族呼吁来推动他的右翼基础投票。

paras.en: “There are buses heading to the polls and long lines in Arab towns. Meanwhile, right-wing strongholds have yet to wake up!” he said on social media. “If we don’t go vote now, we will find ourselves with a government of Arab parties.”
paras.zh: “阿拉伯城镇有前往投票站的巴士和排长队的巴士。与此同时，右翼据点尚未苏醒！”他在社交媒体上说。“如果我们现在不去投票，我们将发现自己与一个由阿拉伯政党组成的政府站在一起。”

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu has a long track record of appealing to his supporters by invoking the specter of the Arab vote. Arab citizens represent about 20 percent of Israel’s population, but have long complained that they are treated as second-class citizens and subject to discrimination.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡在通过援引阿拉伯选票的幽灵来吸引他的支持者方面有着悠久的记录。阿拉伯公民约占以色列人口的20 ％ ，但长期以来一直抱怨他们被当作二等公民对待并受到歧视。

paras.en: In 2015, Mr. Netanyahu called on right-wing Israelis to vote because “Arabs were heading in droves to the polls.” His comments were widely condemned at home and abroad, including by the Obama administration. Mr. Netanyahu was accused of race-baiting and was forced to issue an apology for the remark.
paras.zh: 2015年，内塔尼亚胡呼吁以色列右翼人士投票，因为“阿拉伯人成群结队地前往投票站。他的言论在国内外都受到了广泛的谴责，包括奥巴马政府。内塔尼亚胡先生被指控进行种族诱饵，并被迫为这一言论道歉。

paras.en: On Tuesday, as initial data showed high turnout in Arab cities and towns, Mr. Netanyahu again used almost the same language to vilify Arab voters in several different statements over the course of the day.
paras.zh: 周二，由于初步数据显示阿拉伯城镇的投票率很高，内塔尼亚胡先生在当天的几次不同声明中再次使用了几乎相同的语言来诋毁阿拉伯选民。

paras.en: “They say their voters are heading to the polls in droves. You too must head to the polls in droves,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement, addressing right-wing voters.
paras.zh: “他们说，他们的选民正成群结队地前往投票站。你们也必须成群结队地前往投票站，”内塔尼亚胡在视频声明中对右翼选民说。

paras.en: Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List alliance of Arab parties, accused Mr. Netanyahu of “inciting against Arab citizens and undermining the legitimacy of our vote.”
paras.zh: 领导阿拉伯政党联合名单联盟的尤瑟夫·贾巴林（ Yousef Jabareen ）指责内塔尼亚胡先生“煽动反对阿拉伯公民并破坏我们投票的合法性”。

paras.en: “I’m telling you: the Arab community knows how to punish you,” Mr. Jabareen said. “Today we’re sending you and your bloodstained government packing.”
paras.zh: Jabareen先生说： “我告诉你：阿拉伯社区知道如何惩罚你。” “今天我们送你和你的血迹斑斑的政府包装。”

paras.en: Arab citizens have tended to vote at lower rates than their Jewish counterparts. But in the run-up to this election, surveys suggested that they would turn out in higher numbers in an effort to vote out Mr. Netanyahu and his far-right allies. In Rahat, a large Bedouin town in southern Israel, turnout just before 5 p.m. was already at 60 percent — matching the town’s final turnout in the previous election.
paras.zh: 阿拉伯公民的投票率往往低于犹太公民。但在这次选举前夕，调查显示，他们将以更高的人数投票给内塔尼亚胡及其极右翼盟友。在以色列南部的一个大型贝都因城镇拉哈特，下午5点之前的投票率已经达到60% ，与上次选举中该镇的最终投票率相当。

paras.en: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party and some hard-right ministers in his government have also deployed incendiary messaging to appeal to supporters to vote.
paras.zh: 内塔尼亚胡领导的利库德集团及其政府中的一些强硬派部长也部署了煽动性信息，呼吁支持者投票。

paras.en: The Likud party released images suggesting that there had been higher turnout in the Arab city of Rahat than Bat Yam, a Likud stronghold, which it called “a state of emergency.”
paras.zh: 利库德集团发布的图像显示，阿拉伯城市拉哈特的投票率高于利库德集团的据点巴特亚姆，后者被称为“紧急状态”。

paras.en: Another poster showed women in Muslim religious veils with the caption: “Right-wing voters, don’t stay home.”
paras.zh: 另一张海报展示了戴着穆斯林宗教面纱的女性，上面写着： “右翼选民，不要呆在家里。”

paras.en: Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, joined in the prime minister in trying to stoke fears over high Arab turnout. In a video filmed near the entrance of the Arab town of Kufr Qassim in central Israel, he said that Arab voters were heading to the polls “at hitherto never-before-seen rates,” threatening Israel’s Jewish character.
paras.zh: 极右翼国家安全部长伊塔马尔·本-格维尔（ Itamar Ben-Gvir ）与总理一起试图引发对阿拉伯高投票率的担忧。在以色列中部阿拉伯城镇Kufr Qassim入口附近拍摄的一段视频中，他说，阿拉伯选民正“以前所未有的速度”前往投票站，威胁到以色列的犹太人性格。

paras.en: The prime minister also pointed to the arrests of three people suspected of planning to bribe voters for Raam, an Arab Israeli party, on Tuesday. Dean Livne, the acting director of Israel’s central elections committee, told reporters that there were no reports of widespread irregularities.
paras.zh: 总理还指出，周二逮捕了三名涉嫌计划为阿拉伯以色列政党Raam贿赂选民的人。以色列中央选举委员会代理主任迪恩·利夫内（ Dean Livne ）告诉记者，没有关于普遍存在违规行为的报道。

paras.en: Lia Lapidotand Johnatan Reisscontributed reporting.
paras.zh: Lia Lapidotan和Johnatan重新撰写报告。

paras.en: Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.
paras.zh: 在2023年10月7日哈马斯领导的对以色列的袭击中，几名亲属被杀或被扣为人质，他们正在参加周二的选举，这是自袭击事件以来的首次全国性投票，震撼了该国的基础并引发了最长的战争。

paras.en: The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.
paras.zh: 2023年10月的袭击事件笼罩着本周的投票。在以色列历史上未能防止最严重的军事、情报和政策灾难的责任人问题上，存在着尖锐的分歧。

paras.en: About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.
paras.zh: 据以色列当局称，当天约有1200名平民和士兵被杀，约250人被扣为人质前往加沙。哈马斯劫持的许多人质家属在电视采访和全国抗议活动中为亲人竞选时声名鹊起。

paras.en: Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.
paras.zh: 他们中的大多数人呼吁内塔尼亚胡总理对10月7日的失败负责，并优先谈判释放人质，而不是继续战斗。其他人支持内塔尼亚胡的右翼政府，并敦促它继续对哈马斯和以色列的其他敌人施加军事压力。

paras.en: Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:
paras.zh: 来自以色列各政治派别的政党从10月7日家族中招募了候选人。以下是有机会赢得议会席位的一些候选人：

paras.en: Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.
