articles.title: Ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump goes into effect in Russian-occupied town ‘on the brink of disaster’
articles.author: Yuliya Talmazan

paras.en: A rare humanitarian ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump to save people trapped in a Russian-occupied Ukrainian town went into effect early Tuesday.

After months of warnings from Ukrainian officials about an unraveling humanitarian catastrophe in the front-line town of Oleshky, in the southern Kherson region, the White House announced last week that the first lady had secured a pause in the fighting.

The agreement between Ukraine and Russia would “temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” according to a statement released Friday.

Both the Ukrainian and Russian militaries have confirmed that the ceasefire will start at 3 a.m. local time (9 p.m. ET) to ensure what they have both called a “humanitarian operation.” Neither side has indicated when the temporary truce would end.

The ceasefire announcement came amid renewed pressure from President Donald Trump on his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to reach an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has complained of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S. and a slowdown of Elon Musk’s Starlink service, which is crucial for its military.

Earlier this month, Trump also eased some sanctions on the Kremlin allowing Russia to supply diesel to the global market in an apparent bid to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections, reversing years of American policy — a move that raised alarm in Ukraine and Europe.

But in a rare intervention from the first lady, the White House statement quoted her as saying that Oleshky was “on the brink of disaster” and its remaining population, composed primarily of elderly residents, was in urgent need of medical attention, medicine, food and clean water.

“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks,” she said. “It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”

Civilian representatives from both sides will visit the town, which had a population of around 24,000 people before the war, to determine the level of assistance the remaining residents require, the statement said.
An “impartial American media organization” will document the process to ensure “that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” it added.

The ceasefire is likely to last several days as the Russian side has to “clear the roads of mines,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine’s TSN TV channel Sunday, adding that his forces would have to verify the area is clear.
“There is no doubt that Russia will do everything it can to clear the roads of mines so that these people head toward Russia and stay there. They are not going to simply let people go,” he said.
Both sides blame each other for the crisis in Oleshky.

Kyiv has accused Russian forces of mining nearby roads and using the remaining residents as human shields to prevent Ukraine’s army from conducting offensive operations in the town. Meanwhile, Russia has blamed Ukraine for “laying siege to the town” with drone strikes and preventing humanitarian aid from getting in.
Last month, the Kremlin acknowledged problems with food and medical supplies getting into Oleshky, saying its military was working to resolve them.

Ukrainian media has for months been featuring interviews with people who have managed to escape Oleshky and spoken to relatives of those who remain there — an estimated 2,000 people, including children.
Some said the town was on the verge of starvation and residents were relying on homegrown produce to survive. Others had reportedly resorted to eating grass.
With winter looming, fears of famine are growing in the town where communication is difficult because of a severely compromised internet and cellphone service in the area.
The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, which has been documenting the crisis for months, said there have been no food deliveries to the town since the end of May.
Oleshky, like a large portion of the Kherson region, has been occupied by Russian forces since the early weeks of the invasion.

Drone footage of the town, shared by Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade “Borysfen” last month and verified by NBC News, shows the charred ruins of desolate residential and administrative buildings inside the town, in a rare look at the level of destruction.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, shared another video earlier this month, geolocated by NBC News, showing residents leaving Oleshky on foot, bicycles and mopeds in what he said was a desperate search for food. He said they faced the impossible choice of being blown up on a mine or dying from hunger.

Their plight received international attention in recent weeks after Pope Leo XIV directly raised the growing crisis with Putin, and European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno went on a hunger strike, saying “the people of Oleshky cannot be abandoned.”

While both Kyiv and Moscow have unilaterally announced Easter or Christmas ceasefires before, they did not revolve around a humanitarian crisis and have not involved open mediation by the U.S., making the Oleshky ceasefire an unprecedented halting of fire between the two sides.

The ceasefire could serve as a model for similar humanitarian arrangements in other areas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday, especially given the “highly positive” American involvement, including the first lady.

Melania Trump has been involved in the humanitarian campaign to bring back Ukrainian children taken by Russia, and the White House statement said she leveraged the “communication channel” established through those efforts to bring about a humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky.

articles.title: After days of delay, state regulators confirm probe into methane plume at Chevron
articles.author: Alistair Bates

paras.en: The WA government says it is now actively investigating repeated detections of massive methane clouds above Chevron's Gorgon gas project off the state's Pilbara coast.
Satellite monitoring has picked up on the huge clouds of greenhouse gas for a year, with the United Nations issuing its latest warning in August.
A department spokesperson said it would be "inappropriate" to speculate on the cause of the emissions while the investigation is ongoing.

After days of confusion, the West Australian government has confirmed it is now actively investigating repeated large methane emissions from Chevron's Gorgon gas project off the state's Pilbara coast.

The Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) was initially unclear on whether it had jurisdiction over the plumes, which had been observed by a United Nations-linked satellite for the past year.
But a government spokesperson said DWER was "working hard" to establish the cause of the emissions, and engaging with Chevron to determine the appropriate response.
"It would be inappropriate to speculate while the investigation is underway,"
The Gorgon liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant on Barrow Island is one of the biggest in Australia, boasting a capacity of 15.6 million tonnes per year across its three processing trains.
All of the LNG is shipped overseas. Gorgon hit its 2,000th cargo milestone in February.
About 300 terajoules of Chevron's remaining natural gas is kept for domestic use under the state's reservation policy, which the company says generates enough electricity for 2.5 million households.

In April, the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority (NOPSEMA) accepted Chevron's plans to install a subsea compression station and other infrastructure to maintain production at Gorgon over another 40 years.
Since November last year, five consecutive passes by the Tanager-1 satellite have detected huge methane clouds emerging from the industrial complex.
The most recent posted an emissions rate of 7.8 tonnes of methane an hour near Gorgon's acid gas removal units, making it the highest methane emitter in WA.
Methane is a much more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and responsible for about 25 per cent of global warming.
The UN warned Chevron about its emissions in July last year and as recently as August this year.
The multinational gas giant has not formally provided feedback to the alerts.
Chevron told the ABC it was corresponding with the UN over its data, but did not comment on the state's investigation.
WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill said it was "embarrassing" DWER was not monitoring the emissions and remained noncommittal after they came to light.
"We know that this Labor government has never fined gas companies for these kinds of unauthorised leaks of pollutants," she said.
"This incident proves that the whole system needs to be overhauled."

Pressed during Senate Estimates by independent senator David Pocock, the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment, and Water (DCCEEW) said repeatedly that the oversight of emissions was state-based.
"We're aware of media reports over the last couple of days," said Hew Atkin, DCCEEW's gas and liquid fuels division chief, on Monday.
"My understanding is that's a matter for the state regulator."
Mr Pocock questioned the lack of involvement from the Commonwealth.
"How on earth is this program going to be successful if we don't know about a reportedly massive, unexplained release of methane over the last year or so?"
Chevron is required to report its emissions through the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Scheme. The numbers are published annually.
Australia's current legislated target is to reduce emissions by 43 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030 and achieve net zero emissions by 2050.
According to the UN's International Methane Emissions Observatory, Australia is home to two of the world's top-35 methane emitters as of November.
Both are metallurgical coal mines, Queensland's Moranbah north coal mine, operated by Anglo American, and New South Wales' Appin coal mine, operated by GM3.

articles.title: Echoes from disused water tower become music for 'magical' performance
articles.author: Lily Plass and Lee Brooks

paras.en: High school students in Cobar accompanied a professional string quartet during their performance in a disused water tank.
The students used the natural sounds of sticks, stones and branches to bring the Sound Chapel structure to life.
Some students said the experience inspired them to keep playing music.
Students in outback NSW have woven the echoes of a disused water tower into a unique piece of music.
The structure, known as the Cobar Sound Chapel, is an immersive sound experience.
"When you just walk, you can hear the echo, and it sounds really cool," Year 7 student Indy Webster said.
The music was created during a workshop in Cobar with composer and Sydney Conservatorium lecturer Jim Coyle.
"The students came up with some really excellent ideas, so realising that as a musical score was relatively straightforward," he said.
But Dr Coyle said incorporating a structure into a composition was a first for him as well.
"I tend to use conventional instruments in conventional ways, so this is a whole new area, a breakout, and that's what's particularly exciting about it," he said.
Dr Coyle said music was a universal language.
The Sound Chapel is a permanent sound installation artwork where students from Cobar High recently gathered to perform with the Noise String Quartet and a didgeridoo.
They were encouraged to use the environment around them, including sticks, stones and branches, to create sound.
Music teacher Laura Andrew said she was impressed by the ideas the students came up with.
"You can make art, regardless of your age, and you can still be in school and make real-world creative pieces," she said.
"It was such an amazing experience, just to step back and observe how students came up with different sounds.
"They're celebrating their town, they're celebrating what's here."
Wiradjuri man and former Cobar High School student Xander Jeffery played the didgeridoo during the performance.
He said the sound chapel magnified the acoustic presence of his instrument.
"It creates a huge amount of echo," he said.
"It rings and reverberates and just bounces everywhere."
Mr Jeffery said playing the didgeridoo has helped him reconnect with his culture.
"It's sacred. It's a part of me now," he said.
The Sound Chapel is the work of architect Glenn Murcutt and the music of composer Georges Lentz.
It was created in 2022, although the silver tank itself is 125 years old.
"To see it generating new art out of the Sound Chapel is just so wonderful," Mr Lentz said.
"Having local students and local people invested in this is so important.
"Growing up in Luxembourg, I never dreamt first of coming to Australia, let alone creating something like the Cobar Sound Chapel."
Some audience members travelled hundreds of kilometres to see the students' performance.
Architect Bernie Jovaras and his wife Anne travelled from Victoria to attend and were impressed with what they saw and heard.
"It was really, really sharp and crisp, very little reverberation, and that's due to some clever design elements with the chamber," Mr Jovaras said.
"I thought the sound was absolutely fantastic."
Some of the students left motivated to continue playing music.
"It feels so magical, especially when the music starts to play," Year 9 student Marvelyn Mabhava said.

articles.title: Scammers target major holiday parks across Australia in cybersecurity breach
articles.author: Kristy Sexton-McGrath

paras.en: BIG4 and other major holiday park operators are warning guests about fraudulent messages following a breach involving a third-party booking platform.
Scammers are using booking details to target travellers with fake payment requests.
Travellers are being urged not to click suspicious links or share payment details.
Australian travellers are being warned their personal information may have been exposed following a cybersecurity breach involving an accommodation software company.
Major holiday park operators, including Reflections, BIG4 and G'day Parks, are understood to have been affected through Australian booking management software provider RMS Cloud.
The company provides cloud-based property management and booking systems to more than 6,000 hotels, holiday parks and serviced apartments around the world, according to its website.
The ABC has contacted the company for comment.
One of Australia's biggest holiday parks, BIG4, said guests had been targeted by scammers following a breach of a third-party booking platform.

"We've been made aware of a breach of a third-party platform which is used by some of the parks within our network, as well as a number of other accommodation providers and groups. This has resulted in some guests receiving fraudulent messages asking for credit card or payment details," a Big4 spokeswoman said.

"While RMS is undertaking investigations, we have been in touch with parks who may have been affected and provided them with preliminary information and advice for their customers which includes not clicking on suspicious links or providing payment information."
Reflections Holidays, which runs caravan holiday parks across NSW, has sent guests messages warning them of the scam.

"Our booking system provider RMS has made us aware that there are phishing emails being sent to future Reflections Holidays guests from RMS, claiming booking payments have failed," the text message reads.
"Please don't click links or share payment details."
Cherie Midson, who manages a holiday park in Victoria's East Gippsland, said concerned guests began contacting the business after the messages started circulating.
"The messages started going out last night and the calls started coming in today," Ms Midson said.
"Some of the details, like names and dates of stay, are correct."
Ms Midson said she had reported the matter to the federal government's Scamwatch site.
"It's very worrying. Our details are being used, which reflects on us as a business," she said.
"We're concerned our guests could fall victim to the scam, and if they do, our business will be associated with that. That's a real worry for us."
Summerstar Tourist Parks, which operates dozens of caravan parks across Western Australia, has also warned guests of the "cybersecurity breach" on social media.
"We have recently been notified of a cybersecurity breach from RMS, our external booking system provider," the post says.
"Fraudulent emails and WhatsApp messages that appear to be from Summerstar Tourist Parks are circulating asking you to click a link to verify your booking details."
It is not the first cybersecurity breach to target travellers.
Earlier this year, the ABC revealed Booking.com guests had been targeted in a phishing scam involving fake hotel messages on WhatsApp and emails, with their personal details.
Cybersecurity expert Professor Daswin de Silva said travel data was "highly valuable" because it contained detailed information about a traveller's identify.
"There's an assumption that people who travel have financial capacity, which makes them appealing targets for cybercriminals," he said.
Scamwatch, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's scam reporting service, said it received more than 13,000 reports of phishing scams in the first three months of 2026.

articles.title: Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees
articles.author: Jaspreet ​Singh

paras.en: Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees
Offer will be available to employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States
Microsoft said on Monday it is offering voluntary buyouts to many staff members as the technology giant looks to contain costs and help fund its massive AI investments.

The offer was extended to about 60,000 employees according to Microsoft. The company had 223,000 full-time employees globally as of June 30, according to its annual filing, meaning more than a quarter of its global workforce would have received the buyout offer.

Staffers across the Windows maker would be eligible for the offers, including those working in AI experiences, Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, requesting anonymity as the matter was private. Units such as marketing, commercial business and security will be excluded, the source added.
In a memo, Microsoft's executive vice-president and chief people officer Amy Coleman said the offer will be available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Microsoft declined to tell CBC News how many Canadians were offered the buyout.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a staff memo.

The company said it was a time-limited, voluntary program and built on insights gained from a previous voluntary retirement program. The eligible employees will receive details within the next few hours, it added.

Like other tech giants, Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data centres and chips, drawing scrutiny from investors over whether the returns will justify the staggering cost. The company, slated to report first-quarter results after markets close on Wednesday, has forecast $175 billion US in capital expenditures for the 2026 calendar year.
- Meta to cut 8,000 jobs, Microsoft to offer voluntary buyouts for thousands
- Microsoft to cut 4,800 jobs, overhaul Xbox unit
Shares of Microsoft, which had risen about 10 per cent this year, were up about 1 per cent on Monday. The development was first reported by Business Insider.
The company earlier this year offered voluntary buyouts to about 7 per cent of its U.S. workforce, or about 9,000 employees.

In July, Microsoft announced it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce, overhauling its Xbox gaming business and divesting up to five studios as it looks to boost returns after years of heavy investment in the division.

articles.title: UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce

paras.en: UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce
Israel dismisses report as 'misinformation'

A United Nations commission says Israel continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October's U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, in a report published Monday that Israel dismissed as part of a "misinformation campaign."

The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel examined violations against Palestinian children since the start of the war between Israel and Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, up to September this year.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing "genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza."

The commission also accused Israeli soldiers and prison guards of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases in which Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.

Another report by the commission in September last year found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts — accusations that Israel called scandalous.
The Israeli mission in Geneva said the latest report was part of a misinformation campaign to demonize Israel.

“The attempt to destroy the Jewish state ... continues today through efforts by actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself," Ambassador Daniel Meron said in a statement.
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.

It said the "Yellow Line" which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people, according to Israeli goverment tallies, in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
- Analysis Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st election since Oct. 7
- Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?

In its report to the UN Security Council, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and Oct. 6, 2023, to 254 between Oct. 7, 2023, and Sept. 30, 2026.

Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank formed part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.

Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and human rights defenders had been killed and injured.
- This story has been updated to add attribution to the number of people killed in Israel Oct. 7, 2023.Oct 26, 2026 7:26 PM EDT

articles.title: How this Brooklyn bar owner had Conan O'Brien in stitches on SubwayTakes
articles.author: Marcus Medford-Kerr

paras.en: How this Brooklyn bar owner had Conan O'Brien in stitches on SubwayTakes
Debbie Shields says she had a ball joking with the comedian
It's not everyday you go from running a comedy night at a bar to doing improv with an Emmy-winning comedian on the New York City subway.
Debbie Shields wasn't expecting to strike up a conversation with comedian Conan O'Brien when she set out to run errands, but her quick-witted humour meant she was prepared.
"I mean, if you give it to me, I give it right back to you," she told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
Shields has become an internet sensation after her exchange with O'Brien aired on the most recent episode of SubwayTakes.

O'Brien was a guest on the popular internet talk show hosted by comedian Kareem Rahma, where regular New Yorkers and celebrities humorously discuss their controversial opinions while riding the subway.

Toward the end of his episode, O'Brien apologized to Shields as she moved into an empty seat next to Rahma. She and O'Brien shook hands and jumped into a spontaneous scene together, with O'Brien joking that the two used to be married.
Shields quickly responded that they had two kids. "One's in medical school, the other one's in jail," she said, causing the former late night host to crack up.
Some viewers said they loved her wit and ability to keep up with O'Brien. He was impressed, too.
O'Brien told New York Magazine he's open to working with Shields again. "I'll do a sitcom with her," he said. "Or we can just hit the road, do a two-person show."
Shields told Köksal she'd love to collaborate with him again. Here is part of their conversation.
Debbie, what is your relationship status with Conan O'Brien now? Is remarriage in the cards? He walked out on you again?
He just did his interview and walked off the train. "Bye Debbie."
They're fine. They're used to him not being around.
In all seriousness though, how are you doing with all of this attention?
It's crazy right now. SXM radio, I was in the New York Times, 1010 radio.
Internationally, are they interested, too?
Yeah, somebody called me from Japan, 1:30 in the morning, Australia, England. Oh boy, it's been busy.
On that day on the train, did you have any idea what you were walking into?
Not at all. I was going to see my accountant for my business.
O'Brien appeared delighted with the random encounter. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images/SiriusXM)
Did you just see that shock of orange hair and the pasty skin? He would say that about himself, so I feel like can say that.

No, I saw a camera crew. And when I saw the camera crew, my friend said, "Oh, that's Conan O'Brien." I was like, "Oh, OK." But I was looking for a seat because I'm always looking for a seat on the train. So I got me a seat and I told him "You hold the seat and I'm just going to go over and say hi." And that's all it took.
And you did not miss a beat, a millisecond even. Have you always had that kind of comedic timing?
Yeah, I mean if you give it to me, I give it right back to you. That's how it goes.
That's the New Yorker in you, I would imagine. But you are at another level, though.
You didn't seem nervous, but were you at all nervous inside?
You were a fan of Conan before. What about him do you like?
Yes, I like his style of comedy. He's witty, he's fast, he's risky, he is risque. I just like him.
Did you have any idea about the show SubwayTakes?
No, I didn't know anything about that show, nothing.

It's really cool when you meet a celebrity whose work you admire and the exchange goes really well. Sometimes, it could be not as pleasant. You go about your day, you went to your accountant. And then when did you start getting a sense that this was more than this great memory for you?

Tuesday evening. Somebody told me, "Oh, you're on Conan, we saw it." I was in my bar and people started showing me. Then Wednesday morning, it went crazy. People were calling me at eight in the morning. "Oh, you were all over the internet. You've got five million hits." Then somebody called me at like about 10 in the morning, "You're on television, on channel five. You're on channel four." And I'm like, "Oh my God." It was surreal.

That's what I do with people, even in my bar. The name of my bar is Confessions Bar, I have comedy on Friday nights. I introduce the host of the comics and I really go off on the people. I make them laugh, I talk about their outfits, whatever it is, and they all love me. I like to see people happy. And if I lay my head to rest today, I want people to remember that I made people laugh.
Oh, they're sure going to remember, Debbie. Conan's at the top of that list. Do you think he's going to drop by?
He's been in touch with me. Kareem's team has been in touch with me to do another show with him.
Oh my goodness. What would be your dream show?
I think at least Conan could arrange that for you. Conan said he'd do a sitcom with you.
Yes he would, and I would love to do one with him.

Life is funny, you never know where your blessings are coming from. That's why you have to live your life in a certain way. So when the aura of God, or whatever you want to see or call it, sees that you're doing your best and you're trying really hard and you genuine, he always throws you a ball.
You've got the comedy night at Confessions, are you incorporating this new part of your life and your ex-husband into the bar?
Yes, we invented a drink called Baby Daddy O'Brien. We've got whiskey, Triple Sec, lemon, lime, and blood orange.
Can we expect you to bring your show to Toronto sometime?
That would be fun. I love Toronto. I love Canada. I've been to Canada so many times.
I'm sure people would love to see you riding the subway here, too, Debbie. Thank you for this.
My pleasure. You just always laugh your ass off.

articles.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses

paras.en: Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.

"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.

Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.

"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.

"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."

Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.

The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."

A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?

Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.

Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.

All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.

The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers

Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.

Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.

In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.

"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."

The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.

"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."

But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"

articles.title: Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election

paras.en: Israel is heading to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested election that is being described as one of the most important in its history.

The vote is the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, as well as a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks on Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Qatar.

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to extend his tenure after leading the country’s most right-wing governing coalition which brought together far-right ultranationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza and faced with a long-running corruption trial, he is fighting for his political survival against a self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that has fundamentally embraced a right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges. Questions over accountability for alleged security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab-led parties dominated the campaign.

This has further dampened already low expectations that the vote would offer any meaningful improvement to the lives of Palestinians, as deadly attacks continue almost daily in Gaza despite a yearlong “ceasefire”, while settler pogroms and Israeli army raids have intensified in the occupied West Bank.
“The entire Israeli political system operates within the racist framework of Jewish supremacy,” Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani, a noted Israeli sociologist, told Al Jazeera.

“None of the leaders who present themselves as an alternative to Netanyahu can genuinely be described as left-wing. The horrifying reality we are witnessing is not simply the product of Netanyahu or the far right. It is rooted in Zionist political thought itself, which is structured around the principle of Jewish supremacy. There is no way around this fundamental fact,” he said.

Israel’s shift to the right did not begin with the establishment of Netanyahu’s most recent government in 2022, or what polls show to have been the rightward lurch that took place across Israel following the Hamas-led attack of 2023. Rather, the collapse of the peace process with the Palestinians and repeated security crises over the past few decades have combined to systematically erode the political centre and left, giving rise to landmark legislative milestones such as the 2018 Nation-State Law, which formally enshrined Jewish supremacy and the continued and violent expansion of illegal Israeli settlements into occupied Palestinian territory with little or no government restraint.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: However, if the drift to the right was there beforehand, most analysts agree that its speed has accelerated to unprecedented heights under the latest Netanyahu government, which faced accusations of seeking to reshape the country in its own image

They point to attempts to strip the Supreme Court of its power to review government actions and the flouting of its rulings on conscripting the ultra-Orthodox minority whose political support helped sustain the governing coalition, as well as the presence of figures such as far-right provocateur and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and religious Zionist Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister.

Together, in return for their seat at the table, both ministers offered crucial support to the controversial judicial overhaul that Netanyahu – himself on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, charges he denies – launched in the early months of 2023 and which continues to this day. Similarly, both ministers have provided encouragement and cover for the surge in violence across the West Bank, while deflecting attempts to hold the coalition accountable for the alleged security failures that preceded the Hamas-led attack.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “If Netanyahu loses the election and, say, [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes the new prime minister, the main initial change will be the atmosphere, the vibe, as Netanyahu stirs deep emotions domestically,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

“Those who admire him, and there are many in Israel, regard him as God. Those who hate him, and there are many in Israel, hate him deeply,” said Bregman. “He’s a very divisive figure. A new prime minister is likely to calm things down.”
With the vote closely watched across the region and beyond, analysts also say the stakes go beyond the names on the ballot and cut through to the very nature of the character and future of Israel.

“The decision facing Israel of whether to retain a Netanyahu-led government or not is ultimately the decision on whether to live in a functioning democracy or a democracy in name only,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.

“It’s the choice between maintaining the occupation of the West Bank or annexing it entirely and the population’s ‘voluntary migration’ from there, as figures within the government have actually suggested.”

A respect for process and the rule of law would likely return to government in the event of an opposition win, added Bregman, a sharp contrast with what he described as Netanyahu’s approach to government. However, to expect too great a change in the overall direction of policy would be to miss the point.
“Don’t be mistaken,” he cautioned. “Israel, particularly after 7 October, turned sharply to the right, and any new government will reflect and mirror this reality.”

What will not be on the ballot, analysts and observers say, is any opportunity to challenge a foreign and security policy that has underpinned the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza, the increased violence across the West Bank and the launching of multiple wars, including one on Iran that has seen key energy routes choked and has left global markets reeling.

None of the mainstream candidates for office in October have talked about including Arab-led parties in any potential coalition. In Israel’s popular media, references to the leaders of Ra’am or the Joint List are typically used by rival candidates to denounce each other for considering a future coalition with Palestinian politicians, now or in the past.

Shenhav-Shahrabani, the sociologist, said the ultra-Orthodox parties would still be welcome in government after the vote by either coalition, while the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel – one-fifth of the total population – would be excluded by a system built upon prejudice.

“The distinction is not between democratic and anti-democratic forces, but between Jews and Palestinians. As long as there is no genuine binational political vision, racism and the systematic restriction of Palestinian rights will remain fundamental features of Israeli society,” he said.

If that framework shapes who is allowed into government, it also shapes what the campaign is about. Netanyahu’s challengers largely framed their disagreements with him as questions of competence, timing and accountability for the alleged failures that preceded October 7, rather than challenges to the way Palestinians are treated.

For critics, that omission is not an oversight but a reflection of where the Israeli mainstream now sits: among the issues at stake in the election, none amounted to a referendum on the genocide in Gaza. “How can it be a referendum on genocide, or anything to do with the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza?” asked Daniel Levy, a former Israeli government adviser.

“You would have to have one side arguing it was a good thing and the other arguing it was a bad thing, let alone acknowledging that it was a genocide. So, no, obviously none of that is on the ballot,” he said.

“The treatment of Palestinians by the Israeli state and military is a consensus among Zionist parties,” added Levy, with differences among them primarily resting on “whether it’s the state’s job to oppress Palestinians, or if the settler militias also have a role – a significant role – to play”.

articles.title: Iran, Saudi, Turkiye and Pakistan agree to more talks amid Houthi attacks

paras.en: Saudi Arabia, Iran, Turkiye and Pakistan have agreed to continue talks for regional “peace and security” as the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had intercepted another barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom.

The talks in Tehran on Monday were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations – which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August – since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

In a joint statement issued late on Monday, the four countries “agreed to continue the dialogue to strengthen cooperation amongst the four regional countries, including for peace and security in the region,” according to Iranian state media.

Hours later, early on Tuesday, Colonel Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the coalition, said that three ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis and aimed at Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province had been intercepted, causing no casualties. Four drones headed towards the kingdom’s south were also shot down, he said.
The coalition said it had downed three more drones over Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia on Monday evening.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia said the visit to Tehran was meant to open negotiating channels to “prevent the return of military escalation”. The kingdom sent its defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, a younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Pakistan sent its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey sent its intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin.

Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meetings.

A senior Pakistani security official told the Reuters news agency that the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network. The official said the agenda also covered negotiations between the US and Iran, the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US blockade of Iranian ports.

Another Pakistani official told Reuters that Field Marshal Munir, with US President Donald Trump’s blessing to pursue diplomacy, had presented Iran with a proposal that would offer something to both Washington and Tehran. The agency said the official did not give details.
The states in the Mecca pact, along with Qatar, could act as guarantors if the proposal was accepted, the official said.

Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, meanwhile said the visit showed that “American threats have little impact on countries around the world”. He also spoke of a “new and positive atmosphere” in the region.

Esmaeil Baghaei, a spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, had said earlier that the meeting, proposed when Field Marshal Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards regional security arrangements.
The talks came as tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened recently, with Trump saying on Friday the US may strike Iran again.

Mediation led by Pakistan and Qatar had produced an interim peace agreement in June, but fighting between Iran and the US soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, opening a new front and deepening the humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

The Houthis seized strategic areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government forces in a lightning offensive last month, prompting a counteroffensive. Saudi Arabia has since intensified its strikes on the group.

The Houthis have also struck Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities. An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.

Earlier on Monday, the Houthis claimed another attack on the Riyadh airport as well as crude oil pumping stations in the west and east of Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said the missiles were intercepted and destroyed.
It also said it launched retaliatory attacks, destroying five tunnels used to store ballistic missiles, four missile launchers and a missile depot.
The wider war has also restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and driven up oil and petrol prices.
Egypt, a major financial and political partner of Saudi Arabia, has also moved closer to the fight. Its Parliament on Monday authorised the military to help defend the kingdom.

articles.title: AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says

paras.en: OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.
The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.
Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.

Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.
Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.
“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.

“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”
Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.
“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.
“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”
“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”

According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous [proof of the] existence” of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.
The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.
The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.

While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.
“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.
“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.

“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.

Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR, the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.
Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.
While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.

articles.title: 'The smell of freedom': Serbia's student movement celebrates election triumph
articles.author: Guy De Launey

paras.en: 'The smell of freedom': Serbia's student movement celebrates election triumph

BELGRADE, Serbia — There are no Monday morning blues in Serbia's capital, Belgrade. Cars driving past the green-domed National Assembly sound their horns in celebration. Broadly smiling pedestrians cheer and wave a three-fingered salute in response. This has long been viewed as a nationalist gesture — but now it is the symbol of the Student List.

The group of candidates selected by Serbia's long-running, youth-led protest movement was No. 3 on the ballot in Sunday's parliamentary elections but very much top of the pile when it came to the outcome. The Student List claimed more than half the votes, pushing Serbia's long-serving populist leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) into a distant second place.
In the park opposite the National Assembly, hundreds of volunteers are cleaning up the mess left behind by a pro-government camp that had made the area a no-go zone for most citizens.

"Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom," says one of the volunteers, Radomir Delic, who has been painstakingly picking cigarette butts from the grass. "We are in garbage, but it's the smell of freedom."

Most of the country's opposition parties had stood aside to allow the Student List a clear run. When Vučić conceded defeat, shortly after the polls closed, the crowds on the streets erupted in celebration. Champagne corks popped, fireworks crackled and motorbike engines revved to mosquito pitch. Since then, the revelry has barely paused.

It now seems hard to believe that with no reliable opinion polls, the result had been difficult to call before the election. The Student List was an entirely new proposition, with no hierarchy, no leader and no political experience. It was up against a wily and experienced operator in Vučić. He had served as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since his SNS took power in 2012, but it had always been clear that he was the man in charge.

Vučić was also adept at currying international favor. He maintained Serbia's long-standing friendship with Russia, exchanging multiple official visits with Russian President Vladimir Putin. But he also opened membership talks to join the European Union and pushed for closer relations with the United States.

The latter resulted in considerable controversy when Vučić struck a deal with President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner to build a Trump International Hotel on the site of government buildings bombed by U.S. warplanes in 1999. The legal fallout led to Kushner's withdrawal.

Vučić had cast himself as the strong leader who was taking Serbia forward. But that image sustained an irreparable blow in November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at a recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad, killing 16 people.

The facility had been part of Vučić's signature infrastructure project: the high-speed railway line linking Belgrade with neighboring Hungary's capital, Budapest. The disaster triggered protests, with demonstrators accusing him of presiding over endemic corruption — and led to the creation of the Student List.
Its new members of parliament range from academics to athletes, with a smattering of economists and engineers. But there is still a big question mark over how they might govern.

"The danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory," warns Kurt Bassuener, the co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, a regional think tank. He adds that "it is far from clear to me who's going to be in what position" in the new government.
That, perhaps, is a problem for another day. For now, the smell of victory is still in the air, and the party in Belgrade continues.

articles.title: A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections
articles.author: Itay Stern

paras.en: A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections
TEL AVIV, Israel — Israel is holding pivotal elections on Tuesday in what many Israelis call the most consequential vote in their country's history after the last few years of war.

Polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu trailing in the race behind his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. But it may take weeks or months before it's clear who will be designated the winner.

That's because voters will not directly choose between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Instead, they will vote for one of a dozen main parties running for office in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
The real contest will begin after election day, when party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.
Here is a guide to the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking another term in office.

Netanyahu has led the most right-wing government in Israel's history. His coalition has included Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, leaders of far-right, religious nationalist parties that are also running in this election, as well as two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Netanyahu has led Israel through more than three years of war and regional conflict, from the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza to fighting involving Lebanon, Iran, Syria and Yemen. He is campaigning on Israel's military achievements and his close relationship with President Trump, who recently endorsed him. Netanyahu has also made confronting Iran, and ultimately seeking the fall of its regime, a central part of his campaign.

His principal challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israeli military who is running for prime minister for the first time as the leader of a new center-right party called Yashar, Hebrew for "Straight" or "Upright."

Eisenkot's son, Gal, an Israeli soldier, was killed in Gaza during the war. Recent polls have shown Eisenkot has the strongest chance of replacing Netanyahu, although no party or political bloc appears assured of winning a parliamentary majority.

Eisenkot's Yashar includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
How could Arab parties play a role in the results?

Two predominantly Arab parties are also running, including the United Arab List, also known as Ra'am, which made history in 2021 as the first Arab Islamist party to join an Israeli governing coalition. The party says it is willing to work with predominantly Jewish parties in exchange for policies fighting crime and promoting housing, infrastructure and other problems facing Israel's Arab minority community, which makes up about 20 percent of the country's population.

But nearly all the main predominantly Jewish political parties, including Eisenkot's, remain reluctant to rely on Arab parties to form a coalition. That reluctance could leave the anti-Netanyahu camp without the 61 seats it needs for a governing majority.

Accountability for Oct. 7: The Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage, looms over the election. Netanyahu has resisted calls to establish a state commission of inquiry into the political and security failures that preceded the attack. Eisenkot and other opposition leaders say they would establish such a commission soon after taking office.

Who should serve in the military: Nearly three years of fighting across several fronts have placed a heavy burden on Israel's standing army and military reservists. The military says it needs additional personnel, intensifying a decades-old dispute over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. Netanyahu, reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties for political support, has resisted enlisting them, while Eisenkot is campaigning to expand military service to more ultra-Orthodox Jews.

Israel's judiciary: Before the Oct. 7 attack, Netanyahu's government pursued a judicial overhaul that would have weakened the supreme court and given the governing coalition greater influence over the appointment of judges. The plan triggered some of the largest protests in Israel's history. Netanyahu's far-right partners are campaigning on renewed efforts to limit the power of the courts, while Eisenkot advocates for an independent and powerful judiciary. Netanyahu remains on trial for corruption, and says the charges are politically motivated.

paras.en: The wars in Gaza and the region, and Israel's policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many governments overseas, and public support for Israel in the U.S. has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters. Netanyahu emphasizes his relationship with Trump and argues that military strength has improved Israel's strategic position. Eisenkot and his allies say continued international isolation threatens Israel's economy, diplomatic relationships and security.
A party does not need to finish first in the race for the party leader to be Israel's next prime minister. What matters is whether he can assemble a coalition with majority support in parliament.
Most recent polls suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to a majority. That leaves several possible outcomes:

- Eisenkot's allies could break their campaign promises and form a coalition relying on support from one or more Arab parties, either as formal coalition members or from outside the coalition, and the opposition would rule with a minority government
- Netanyahu and Eisenkot could form a broad unity government, although Eisenkot has publicly ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
- Netanyahu could agree to a plea deal that would dismiss his criminal charges in court, in exchange for stepping down as prime minister and serving under Eisenkot as a senior minister.
- A deadlock, where neither side may be able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.

Even if Eisenkot cannot immediately form a coalition, a parliamentary majority opposed to Netanyahu could try to elect a new Knesset speaker, establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks, and advance legislation on ultra-Orthodox military service.

Netanyahu would try to do everything he can to prevent such an outcome. His Likud party's billboards are already promoting a scenario in which the party could claim that the election was stolen, a move that could lead to chaos in the days after the vote.
What direction would Israel take depending on who wins the election?

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently supports the establishment of a Palestinian state in the foreseeable future. Their most significant differences concern democratic institutions, the occupied West Bank and Israel's relationship with the world.

Netanyahu has governed with ultra-Orthodox and far right parties that support settlement expansion in the West Bank and a weaker supreme court. His far-right partners have pushed for annexation of the West Bank and expulsion of Palestinians, drawing sanctions from the U.K. and Europe.

Eisenkot presents himself as a more institutional and pragmatic alternative. He has also taken a tougher position against violence by Israeli settlers and says he would act against settlement outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.

Eisenkot has opposed settlement construction in E1, a strategically sensitive area just east of Jerusalem. Critics of the settlement plan say Israeli construction there would further divide the West Bank and make the creation of a territorially contiguous Palestinian state much more difficult.

The choice facing Israeli voters is therefore not a straightforward contest between left and right. It is also a contest over Netanyahu's leadership, accountability for Oct. 7, the role of religion in the state, the independence of Israel's institutions and what kind of alliances the country will pursue at home and abroad.
NPR's Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

articles.title: Brewers ride ridiculous, record-setting eight-run inning to dominant 3-0 World Series lead over Rays

paras.en: The Milwaukee Brewers moved one step closer to their first ever World Series title on Monday night, taking a 3-0 series lead with a dominant 10-1 win.

That's the short version of the story. The long version? The Tampa Bay Rays will be kicking themselves over a disastrous top of the fifth inning, and historians will one day use a clip of that inning, and the entire 2026 Brewers' postseason run for that matter, as proof of how powerful luck is in Major League Baseball.

Game three meant the series shifted to Tampa Bay, and Tropicana Field was packed to the rafters with Rays fans and a sizable contingent of Brewers supporters. But as has typically been the case this postseason, only those in Milwaukee blue and gold had much to cheer about.

At least defensively, the Rays put up a fight. In the top of the second, outfielder Chandler Simpson made a tremendous running catch in the left field corner, crashing into the fence to rob Sal Frelick of a hit. Then catcher Nick Fortes caught Garrett Mitchell trying to steal second base to end the inning. It was all downhill from there.

In the third inning, the Milwaukee superteam machine kicked into high gear. Jackson Chourio started things off with a ground ball single. Jake Bauers followed with a walk. That's when the Brewers' incredible penchant for outperforming on batting average on balls in play reared its gigantic head yet again.
Christian Yelich popped up a 71 mph blooper that fell in for an RBI single. William Contreras followed with another 79 mph blooper that fell in to drive in the second run of the game.

Still, a 2-0 game in the third inning wouldn't normally mean that much, but the Brewers had Robert Gasser on the mound. Who's Robert Gasser you might be wondering? Well, essentially the epitome of a league average pitcher, someone who had a 4.27 "expected" ERA in the regular season, then turned into a Cy Young candidate in the playoffs. Because baseball.

Gasser entered his game three start with just one run allowed in the playoffs, but the Rays couldn't muster even that on Monday night. Rarely getting swings and misses, Gasser relied on his best friend in October: the opposing team having exceptionally poor luck on batted balls put in play. Prior to Monday, opposing hitters had just a .185 BABIP against him. Then he went six shutout innings with just three strikeouts and only one hit allowed. How? Because the Rays had an .071 BABIP. Gasser will likely end his postseason with just seven hits on 55 balls put in play, an incredible .127 batting average allowed, when league average is around .300.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Gasser's start was the first time a lefty had gone six shutout innings while facing the minimum number of hitters in the World Series since Sandy Koufax.

Next time you want your favorite team to acquire the big name starting pitcher in free agency or at the trade deadline, just remember that one of the most effective starters on the team that won the World Series was Robert Gasser. That he did something that hadn't been done in the World Series by a lefty since one of the greatest pitchers in the history of the sport. In large part because of BABIP. There's no luck in baseball, because everything must have an explanation, no matter how absurd.

Gasser didn't need much support, obviously, but the Brewers unstoppable offense provided it anyway. In the fifth inning, Milwaukee put together one of the most absurd innings you'll ever see, and a near-perfect reminder of the immense amount of variance and randomness inherent in baseball.

It started innocently enough, with Chourio once again singling with one out. Jake Bauers flew out for the second out, then Christian Yelich walked to put runners at first and second. Then, the play that will haunt Rays fans forever.

William Contreras grounded one in the hole between second and third, and third baseman Junior Caminero went to second base for the force out, unable to see that he had plenty of time to get Contreras at first. But Yelich beat the throw out, loading the bases for Brice Turang. Then, the floodgates opened.

Turang hit a grounder to short that Taylor Walls couldn't make the play on, scoring two. Then Garrett Mitchell slapped another single through the infield, directly where the shortstop typically plays. 5-0 Milwaukee. Cooper Pratt followed with a grounder that somehow clipped the foul line for a double, making it 7-0. Sal Frelick hit a soft line drive that fell in to left field to make it 8-0. David Hamilton, having an incredible postseason after a career of being a very bad hitter, drove in the ninth run of the game with a single. Finally, Jackson Chourio added his fourth hit of the game and second of the inning to make it 10-0. Why not?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That fifth inning was the first eight-run inning in World Series history. The Brewers went 9-18 with runners in scoring position, had a .471 BABIP and 16 hits against a typically strong Rays pitching staff. Tampa's BABIP? .130. That's only half of it. Per the league's Statcast page, Milwaukee's expected batting average in the game was .254. Their actual batting average was .390. Tampa's expected batting average was .236, and their actual was .107. And that's been Milwaukee's luck all postseason.

The Rays added a meaningless garbage time run in the bottom of the ninth, but Milwaukee takes a commanding 3-0 series lead, and is well on their way to the organization's first ever championship. Potentially as soon as Tuesday night's game four.

Should the Brewers close it out with a fully rested bullpen, they'd become the first team in the history of the sport to sweep both the NLCS and World Series. They're 10-1 in the playoffs thus far, with a chance to go 11-1 and win ten of nine straight to win a title. Baseball-ruining superteam indeed.

Not all of these results are down to luck, of course, and it's hardly a criticism of the Brewers' team or players to say they've had fortune on their side in the playoffs. Every team that wins the playoff tournament in Major League Baseball has luck go their way. The Dodgers in 2024 and 2025 had plenty of breaks, as did the Rangers in 2023 and Astros in 2022. And the Braves in 2021 and so on.

But there's an inescapable conclusion from this World Series, and the whole postseason, as a matter of fact: there is no way to "ruin" baseball. Or build a superteam. Or guarantee a championship. Because at the end of the day, the gaps between teams are so small that a few bounces either way over a short series can, and often does, determine the outcome. Having a rotation filled with Cy Young level pitchers is great and all, except that when it comes down to it, Robert Gasser can become Sandy Koufax over 15 innings. There's no way to predict who will get hot, who will be cold, and which teams will have luck on their side. Which is what baseball has always been, and always will be. No matter how much fake complaining owners do.
